Functionality is broken despite green status indicators. The failure is in the flow, not the components.

domains.name: Start Here: Your First Session
domains.description: How this bootcamp works, how to study with it, and what the assessment measures. Complete this domain first.

scenarios.title: Maya's first session
scenarios.situation: Maya opens the bootcamp with a Terraform interview in 60 days. She reads four lessons in a row, nods along, and closes the tab feeling productive. She has not opened the Terminal tab or attempted any scenario.
scenarios.prompt: What is the most important correction to Maya's approach?
evidence: Lessons read: 4 | Scenarios attempted: 0 | Labs run: 0 | terraform commands run: 0
The loop is learn → apply → build. Interviews test applied judgment with configs and plans, not lesson familiarity.
choices: She must complete the loop: after lessons, work scenarios (infrastructure judgment) and run labs in the terminal (CLI muscle memory) — interviews expose lesson-only knowledge within minutes, and only the full loop builds it.
She should read faster — four lessons is too slow.
Her approach is fine — understanding the ideas is what interviews test.
She should skip to the mock assessment immediately to save time.
scenarios.why: Whether she can read a plan and reason about state — lesson familiarity produces fluent nods and zero CLI fluency. The scenario+lab loop converts reading into the applied judgment interviews probe. Choice 2 confuses speed with learning. Choice 3 misstates what interviews test. Choice 4 skips the learning the mock measures.
scenarios.hint: What will an interviewer discover in the first five minutes?
objectives: Distinguish passive consumption from the learn-apply-build loop

scenarios.title: The comfort-rep trap
scenarios.situation: Aisha's accuracy is 92% in HCL & resources but 55% in state management. Her sessions keep drifting back to HCL scenarios 'because it feels good to get them right.' Interviews are in five weeks.
scenarios.prompt: What is wrong with her allocation?
evidence: Last 6 sessions: 5 HCL blocks, 1 state block.
choices: She is investing where she is already strong — the 55% domain is the leak, and state confusion compounds into every later domain; every session should prioritize a state repair sequence until it crosses 70%.
Nothing — confidence from high accuracy is the best interview asset.
She should quit scenarios and re-read the state lessons.
She should split time evenly across all domains regardless of scores.
scenarios.why: State is load-bearing — workspaces, backends, drift, and collaboration all assume it, so a 55% there infects everything downstream. Choice 2 mistakes confidence for competence. Choice 3 returns to the failed modality. Choice 4 ignores the data.
scenarios.hint: Why is the state-management gap more dangerous than a generic weak domain?

scenarios.title: The mock surprise
scenarios.situation: After all domains, Leo mocks at 58% under timed conditions. Breakdown: iac-concepts 88%, hcl-resources 80%, state-management 72%, workspaces-environments 41%, everything else 60-70%. He considers 're-studying everything' for a month.
scenarios.prompt: What should Leo do?
choices: Run a targeted repair on workspaces-environments — re-learn via worked examples, work all 5 scenarios with explanations, run the workspace labs — while maintaining light review elsewhere; 21 days is enough for a surgical fix.
Re-study every domain equally for a month.
Postpone all interviews by three months.
Re-take the mock immediately — the 41% was probably nerves.
scenarios.why: One clear weak domain against solid others — a surgical repair target. The mock is a work order: fix workspaces, hold the rest. Choice 2 ignores the diagnostic. Choice 3 wastes months on a weeks-sized problem. Choice 4 treats the instrument as a slot machine.
scenarios.hint: What does the breakdown actually show?

scenarios.title: The explanation skipper
scenarios.situation: Marcus works scenarios fast and moves on, reading explanations only after wrong answers — and only the first sentence. Correct answers are never reviewed. His accuracy has plateaued at 68% for three weeks.
scenarios.prompt: What change breaks the plateau?
evidence: Explanations: only after wrong answers, first sentence only.
choices: Read the full explanation after every answer — including correct ones — and restate its core claim as a runbook rule in his notes; right answers for wrong reasons are future outages.
Answer faster — speed is what interviews reward.
Stop using hints — they are making him dependent.
Switch bootcamps — this one stopped working.
scenarios.why: Both outcomes — he skims wrong-answer explanations and never examines correct ones. The protocol requires the full explanation plus restatement after every answer. Choice 2 confuses speed with judgment. Choice 3 misdiagnoses. Choice 4 blames the instrument.
scenarios.hint: What is he not learning from?

scenarios.title: No target, no protocol
scenarios.situation: Jordan is 'learning Terraform in general' with no interview date and no infrastructure goal. His labs are run half-heartedly — 'I'll take it seriously when I need it.' His scenario accuracy drifts at 60%.
scenarios.prompt: What is the root problem?
evidence: No interview date, no infra goal. Labs: half-hearted.
choices: No real target — without a goal (a stack to build, an interview date), there's no scope discipline and no mock that matters; he should pick one (even a personal project: 'my blog infra as code'), let it scope the depth, and treat the mock as real.
Terraform is too hard without a target — he needs easier material.
He needs more lessons before attempting scenarios.
60% is fine for general learning.
scenarios.why: Everything downstream: the capstone becomes a real repo, labs have stakes ('my actual infra'), and the mock measures readiness for something. Targetless study has no definition of done. Choice 2 blames difficulty. Choice 3 adds lessons to a motivation problem. Choice 4 normalizes drift.
scenarios.hint: What would a real target change?
objectives: Connect preparation to a real target

domains.name: Workspaces & Environments
domains.description: Terraform workspaces, environment separation strategies, per-environment variables and backends — and the pitfalls that leak dev into prod.

scenarios.title: The workspace that leaked to prod
scenarios.situation: An engineer runs `terraform apply` intending dev. The shell was in workspace `prod` from yesterday's incident work. The apply modifies production databases. The plan was reviewed — for dev.
scenarios.prompt: What failed, and what is the systemic fix?
evidence: workspace: prod (leftover from yesterday). Engineer believed: dev.
Reviewed against dev expectations; applied to prod.
choices: The environment selection was memory-based — no prompt indicator, no wrapper, no CI gate; the fixes are layered: workspace in the shell prompt, wrapper scripts that bind workspace+backend+tfvars per environment, and CI that derives the target from the branch so humans never select it under pressure.
The engineer — they should have run `terraform workspace show` first.
Workspaces — the feature is too dangerous; delete them.
The plan review — reviewers should have caught it.
scenarios.why: Because it relies on memory under pressure — the exact condition where memory fails. The post-mortem lesson: make the safe path automatic (prompt, wrapper, CI-derived target). Choice 2 repeats the failed control. Choice 3 discards the tool for a UX problem. Choice 4 blames reviewers for an invisible precondition.
scenarios.hint: Why is 'should have checked' not a fix?

scenarios.title: Workspaces or directories?
scenarios.situation: A 40-engineer company with SOC 2 requirements runs dev/staging/prod as Terraform workspaces on one backend with shared credentials. Auditors ask: 'Who can modify production state?' The answer is 'anyone with backend access' — which is everyone.
scenarios.prompt: What is the right architecture here?
evidence: Workspaces on one backend, shared credentials, 40 engineers.
'Who can modify production state?' Answer: everyone.
choices: Separate directories + per-environment backends and credentials — workspaces can't express 'only SREs touch prod state'; per-env backends get per-env IAM, per-env locking, and real blast-radius isolation. Workspaces fit small similar environments, not audited prod.
Keep workspaces — add a policy document saying only SREs use the prod workspace.
One workspace — simplify further.
Move prod to ClickOps — then Terraform can't touch it.
scenarios.why: Access boundaries — a workspace is a state partition, not a permission boundary; everyone with backend access reaches every workspace's state. Choice 2 is a paper control auditors reject. Choice 3 worsens it. Choice 4 abandons IaC for the most critical environment.
scenarios.hint: What can't workspaces provide that the auditors need?

scenarios.title: The tfvars sprawl
scenarios.situation: Environments are configured with heavy `terraform.workspace` branching: `count = workspace == "prod" ? 5 : (workspace == "staging" ? 2 : 1)` repeated across 30 resources. Adding a fourth environment (qa) requires editing 30 blocks. Last week someone edited 29.
scenarios.prompt: What is the structural fix?
evidence: Add qa environment: 29 of 30 blocks updated.
qa is subtly wrong in one resource — found in production.
choices: Move environment differences into variable values: declare variables once, supply per-environment tfvars files — adding qa becomes writing one tfvars file, not editing 30 blocks; the configuration stays identical across environments and CI plans each env from its file.
Be more careful editing — use a checklist for the 30 blocks.
Don't add environments — three is enough.
Write a script to edit the 30 blocks — automate the sprawl.
scenarios.why: Environment differences as code branches — which means every new environment is a code change across N sites, each a chance to miss one. Values-in-tfvars makes environments data, and data doesn't need 30 edits. Choice 2 checklists the sprawl. Choice 3 refuses to grow. Choice 4 automates the wrong pattern.
scenarios.hint: What does the ternary sprawl actually encode?

scenarios.title: The shared state key
scenarios.situation: Two teams copy-pasted the backend block; both configurations use key `prod/terraform.tfstate` in the same bucket. Team B's apply overwrites Team A's state. Team A's next plan wants to destroy everything — 'it thinks nothing exists.'
scenarios.prompt: What happened, and how is it prevented?
evidence: Team B's apply overwrote Team A's state file.
Team A plans mass destruction — state no longer matches their reality.
choices: State key collision — two configurations claimed one key, so the second apply replaced the first's state; prevention is key naming conventions (team/service/env in the key) enforced by CI checks that reject duplicates, plus separate buckets or prefixes per team.
Team B is at fault — they should have asked first.
S3 is eventually consistent — wait and it resolves.
Team A should re-import everything — that's the fix.
scenarios.why: That applies don't overwrite each other's memory — the state file is per-configuration by design, and sharing a key merges two realities into one file. Choice 2 blames people for a missing convention. Choice 3 misdiagnoses (S3 is read-after-write consistent; this is a keying error). Choice 4 treats the symptom after the corruption.
scenarios.hint: What does one key per configuration guarantee?

scenarios.title: The Friday destroy
scenarios.situation: An engineer runs `terraform destroy` in what they believe is the dev workspace, cleaning up after testing. It was prod. There is no approval gate, no backup of state, and the destroy required only typing 'yes.'
scenarios.prompt: What layered defenses would have prevented this?
evidence: terraform destroy — typed 'yes'. Believed workspace: dev. Actual: prod.
None: no approval, no state backup, no prompt indicator.
choices: Multiple: workspace in the prompt (visibility), wrapper scripts per environment (no manual selection), CI-only applies/destroys for prod (no CLI destroys), state versioning/backups (recovery), and a manual approval gate for destroy plans — no single layer is enough.
Better engineers — hire people who check first.
Remove `terraform destroy` — the command shouldn't exist.
Type 'yes' more carefully — the confirmation is the safeguard.
scenarios.why: It confirms intent, not correctness — the engineer fully intended to destroy; they were just wrong about WHERE. Every layer that was missing (prompt, wrapper, CI gate, backup) addresses a different failure mode. Choice 2 hires against human fallibility. Choice 3 removes a legitimate tool. Choice 4 mistakes the confirmation's purpose.
scenarios.hint: Why isn't the 'yes' confirmation sufficient?

domains.name: Providers Deep Dive
domains.description: Provider blocks, version pinning, aliases for multi-region and multi-account, authentication, and debugging provider issues.

scenarios.title: The unpinned provider
scenarios.situation: A configuration has no `required_providers` version constraint. Monday's `terraform init` pulls AWS provider 6.0 (major release); plans now show hundreds of diffs from renamed arguments. Friday's apply used 5.x.
scenarios.prompt: What went wrong, and what is the fix?
evidence: Provider 5.x, clean plan. Monday: 6.0, hundreds of diffs (renamed arguments).
choices: Unpinned provider + uncommitted lock file — every init could resolve a new major; the fix is a version constraint (`~> 5.0`) in required_providers, the committed lock file pinning exact builds, and treating the 6.0 upgrade as a migration (changelog, dev first), not an accident.
The provider team — major releases shouldn't rename arguments.
Monday — don't run init on Mondays.
Accept the diffs — apply them; renames are harmless.
scenarios.why: 'Any version, forever' — including future breaking majors. The constraint is the contract; the lock file is the receipt. Choice 2 blames the releaser for the team's missing pin. Choice 3 is superstition. Choice 4 applies hundreds of unreviewed changes.
scenarios.hint: What did 'no constraint' actually mean?

scenarios.title: The credentials in the provider block
scenarios.situation: A provider block contains `access_key = "AKIAIOSFODNN7EXAMPLE"` and `secret_key = "..."`. The repo is public on GitHub. The keys have been there for 8 months.
scenarios.prompt: What is the response?
choices: Treat as an active breach: rotate the credentials immediately, purge from git history, audit CloudTrail for misuse over the 8 months, then move to workload identity / SSO / OIDC federation so no long-lived secrets exist to leak — and add secret scanning to CI.
Delete the lines — the keys are old, probably fine.
Make the repo private — that fixes it.
Change the keys next sprint — it's on the backlog.
scenarios.why: Git history is forever — the keys are in every clone and in the public record; only rotation kills them, and 8 months of CloudTrail needs review because the keys were usable the whole time. Choice 3 closes the barn door after 8 months. Choice 4 schedules the breach response for later.
scenarios.hint: Why is 'delete the lines' insufficient?

scenarios.title: The alias that wasn't passed
scenarios.situation: A module creates buckets in a second region via `provider = aws.west`, but the module block doesn't pass the aliased provider. Plan fails: 'provider configuration not present' — a cryptic error referencing the module's internals.
scenarios.prompt: What is the fix?
choices: Pass the alias explicitly: `providers = { aws.west = aws.west }` in the module block, with `configuration_aliases = [aws.west]` declared in the module's required_providers — modules don't inherit caller aliases; the wiring is explicit by design.
Define the aliased provider inside the module — modules should be self-contained.
Remove the alias — put everything in one region.
The error is a Terraform bug — work around it with two configs.
scenarios.why: Encapsulation — modules declare their provider needs via configuration_aliases, and the caller wires them; implicit inheritance would make modules' requirements invisible. The explicit `providers` map is the contract. Choice 2 duplicates provider config per module (drift). Choice 3 abandons the topology. Choice 4 mislabels the design.
scenarios.hint: Why doesn't the module see the caller's alias?

scenarios.title: The 403 on apply
scenarios.situation: Plan succeeds; apply fails with 403 on every resource. The credentials work for reads (plan) but the deploy role lacks write permissions. The role was scoped last quarter in a least-privilege exercise.
scenarios.prompt: What is the diagnosis and fix?
evidence: Deploy role scoped down last quarter (least privilege).
choices: Authorization, not authentication — the credential chain works (plan reads fine); the role's policy denies writes. The fix is scoping the role to exactly what the configuration manages (plan the permission set from the resource types), tested with a plan+apply in dev — least privilege needs to include the writes Terraform performs.
The credentials are wrong — regenerate them.
Terraform is broken — plan shouldn't succeed if apply can't.
Give the role AdministratorAccess — least privilege failed.
scenarios.why: Reads were permitted — the scoping exercise kept read permissions and cut writes, so plan (read-heavy) passed while apply (write-heavy) hit 403s. Plan success never implies apply permission. Choice 2 regenerates working credentials. Choice 3 misunderstands plan's read-only nature. Choice 4 swings from scoped to `*`.
scenarios.hint: Why did plan succeed?

scenarios.title: The inconsistent result
scenarios.situation: After apply, Terraform reports: 'Provider produced inconsistent result after apply' for an instance's `user_data`. The plan showed the script; the API normalized it (trailing newline stripped). Every subsequent plan shows a diff.
scenarios.prompt: What is the fix?
evidence: API stripped the trailing newline; config still has it.
choices: Align the configuration with the API's normalization — remove the trailing newline (or use a function/normalizer the provider documents) so config matches what the API stores; the perpetual diff is config-vs-reality disagreement, and reality wins.
Ignore it — perpetual diffs are harmless.
Report a provider bug — the provider should preserve the newline.
Taint the instance on every apply — force recreation to clear it.
scenarios.why: Config vs prior state vs API reality — and the API normalized the value, so config and reality permanently disagree. The fix is making the config express what the API stores. Choice 2 normalizes noise that hides real diffs. Choice 3 might be valid upstream, but you need the diff gone today. Choice 4 recreates infrastructure to fix a newline.
scenarios.hint: What is the plan actually comparing?

domains.name: Testing & Validation
domains.description: Validate, plan review, static analysis, policy as code, and integration testing — catching infrastructure bugs before apply.

scenarios.title: The plan nobody read
scenarios.situation: An engineer runs `terraform apply` and approves the plan after glancing at the resource counts: '47 to add, looks right.' Buried in the output: 1 to destroy — the production database, being replaced due to a changed attribute that forces replacement.
scenarios.prompt: What is the review failure, and what process prevents it?
evidence: 47 to add, 12 to change, 1 to destroy.
Production database — replacement forced by a changed attribute.
Counts glanced at; the destroy not noticed.
choices: Counts-only review — the summary hides WHICH resources change; the process is the four-check plan review (counts, no unexpected destroys, changed attributes intended, outputs sane) plus tooling that highlights destroys, and policy blocking unapproved database replacement.
The engineer is careless — hire better reviewers.
47 adds is too many — smaller applies.
Terraform shouldn't allow destroys — disable them.
scenarios.why: Nothing — the summary is not the plan. The destroy was visible in the full output; the review never looked. Destroys deserve their own explicit confirmation, and databases deserve policy gates. Choice 2 blames the human for a missing process. Choice 3 shrinks the apply instead of fixing review. Choice 4 removes a legitimate operation.
scenarios.hint: What does '47 to add' tell you about the 1 destroy?

scenarios.title: The validate that passed
scenarios.situation: `terraform validate` passes. `terraform plan` fails: the AMI ID doesn't exist in the region, and a variable value violates an AWS limit. 'But validate said it was fine!'
scenarios.prompt: Why did validate pass, and what catches these?
evidence: Fails: AMI not found in region; variable violates AWS limit.
choices: Validate checks HCL coherence, not cloud reality — it never calls APIs, so unknown AMI IDs and service limits are invisible to it; plan (which refreshes and queries providers) catches them, which is why the pipeline is fmt → validate → tflint/checkov → plan, each stage catching what the last can't.
Validate is broken — file a bug.
The AMI should be hardcoded — then validate would catch it.
Skip validate — it's useless if plan catches everything.
scenarios.why: fmt: 'is it canonical?' validate: 'is the HCL coherent?' tflint/checkov: 'does it follow rules?' plan: 'what will the cloud do?' Each stage sees what the previous can't — that's the point of layering. Choice 2 blames the tool for its documented scope. Choice 3 hardcodes the problem. Choice 4 removes the cheapest gate.
scenarios.hint: What question does each stage answer?

scenarios.title: The open bucket in the scan
scenarios.situation: checkov flags an S3 bucket: 'S3 bucket has public ACL.' The engineer adds `#checkov:skip=CKV_AWS_20` with no ticket and no expiry. Six months later the bucket — public, with customer exports — is found by a researcher.
scenarios.prompt: What is the process failure?
evidence: #checkov:skip=CKV_AWS_20 — no ticket, no expiry, no review.
Public bucket with customer data, found externally.
choices: Unjustified permanent skip — skips must carry a ticket, an expiry, and a reviewer; an unjustified skip is a vulnerability with a comment. The scanner found it; the process buried it. Policy-as-code gates would have blocked the apply regardless of the scan's skip.
checkov is too strict — public buckets are sometimes fine.
The researcher — they shouldn't scan other people's buckets.
S3 — buckets shouldn't be public by default.
scenarios.why: A permanent exception granted by whoever typed it — no review, no expiry, no accountability. The scanner did its job; the human overrode it without process. Choice 2 defends the misconfiguration. Choice 3 blames the finder. Choice 4 is true but irrelevant — the config chose public.
scenarios.hint: What is a skip comment without a ticket?

scenarios.title: The untested module
scenarios.situation: A shared VPC module used by 12 teams gets a 'small cleanup' PR: a renamed output. It merges with no tests. All 12 downstream configurations break on next plan — the output name changed, and nothing caught it.
scenarios.prompt: What would have caught this, and what is the rule?
evidence: 12 downstream configs broken on next plan.
choices: Contract tests on the module — `terraform test` assertions on outputs (and plan-level tests) would fail the PR before merge; the rule is that shared-module interfaces are versioned contracts: renames are breaking changes requiring a major version bump and migration notes, never a 'cleanup.'
The 12 teams — they should pin their module versions.
Code review — a human would have caught the rename.
Don't clean up shared modules — leave them alone forever.
scenarios.why: Downstream configurations reference it by name — the rename breaks every caller at plan time. Module interfaces are APIs; the test suite is the contract enforcement. Choice 2 helps (pinning limits blast radius) but doesn't catch the break. Choice 3 might catch it, might not — tests catch it always. Choice 4 freezes shared code forever.
scenarios.hint: Why is a renamed output a breaking change?

scenarios.title: The apply that 'succeeded'
scenarios.situation: `terraform apply` exits 0. The engineer closes the laptop. An hour later: the app is down — the new instances never passed health checks; the load balancer has no healthy targets. Terraform did exactly what was asked; what was asked was wrong.
scenarios.prompt: What is missing from 'done'?
evidence: Instances unhealthy; LB has zero healthy targets; app down.
choices: Post-apply verification — exit 0 means Terraform's API calls succeeded, not that the system works; done = outputs as expected + smoke tests green + health checks passing + monitoring quiet. The pipeline should verify automatically; the runbook should verify manually.
Terraform — it should check health itself.
The engineer — they should have watched longer.
Health checks — remove them; they caused the outage.
scenarios.why: That the API calls succeeded — nothing about the application's health. 'Terraform applied' and 'the system works' are different claims; verification bridges them. Choice 2 expands Terraform's job into deployment verification. Choice 3 asks humans to stare at dashboards indefinitely. Choice 4 removes the detector that found the problem.
scenarios.hint: What does exit 0 actually certify?
objectives: Define done as healthy, not exit-0

domains.name: Enterprise Patterns
domains.description: Repo layouts, remote state at scale, tagging governance, cost estimation, and team workflows for Terraform in organizations.

scenarios.title: The monorepo meltdown
scenarios.situation: One Terraform monorepo, one pipeline, 60 engineers. A networking change and an app change merge within minutes; the single pipeline applies both. The app change had a typo — the pipeline fails halfway, leaving the network half-applied and the app unapplied. Rollback is unclear: which half do you revert?
scenarios.prompt: What is the structural problem?
evidence: One monorepo, one pipeline, 60 engineers, all stacks.
Two unrelated changes, one pipeline run, partial failure.
choices: Blast radius coupling — unrelated stacks share a pipeline and a failure domain, so one typo poisons an unrelated apply and rollback is ambiguous; the fix is partitioning by blast radius (per-domain repos or per-stack pipelines with independent applies), so failures are contained and reverts are obvious.
The typo — better engineers wouldn't typo.
Monorepos are bad — split into 60 repos.
Pipelines are bad — go back to CLI applies.
scenarios.why: Shared fate — two independent changes rode one pipeline run, so 'revert' has no clean meaning. Blast-radius partitioning (per-stack pipelines at minimum) makes each apply independently revertable. Choice 2 blames the typo for the coupling. Choice 3 overcorrects to repo-per-person. Choice 4 abandons automation for the incident it was preventing.
scenarios.hint: What made the rollback ambiguous?

scenarios.title: The untagged fleet
scenarios.situation: Finance asks: 'Which team owns the $48,000/mo in EC2?' The fleet is 70% untagged — tags were 'recommended' in the wiki. Nobody can allocate the cost, and the optimization project stalls: you can't optimize what you can't attribute.
scenarios.prompt: What is the fix?
choices: Mandatory tags enforced in code: default_tags in provider blocks + policy-as-code blocking untagged resources, with the 4-5 tag set (Owner, Environment, CostCenter, ManagedBy) — then activate cost allocation tags in the billing console and attribute the $48k. 'Recommended' is the failure mode.
Ask teams nicely to tag — a campaign with stickers.
Estimate the attribution — 70% guess is fine.
Tags don't matter — just cut everything 10%.
scenarios.why: Because optional doesn't happen at scale — enforcement (default_tags + blocking policy) is the only mechanism that works across teams and time. Choice 2 repeats the failed approach with stickers. Choice 3 guesses at $48k. Choice 4 cuts blindly, including the things that earn money.
scenarios.hint: Why did 'recommended' produce 70% untagged?

scenarios.title: The state bucket without versioning
scenarios.situation: An engineer accidentally deletes the production state file from the S3 backend (wrong bucket in a cleanup script). Versioning was never enabled. The infrastructure still exists — but Terraform's memory of it is gone. Recovery is manual import of 400 resources.
scenarios.prompt: What are the layered fixes?
evidence: State file deleted by a cleanup script (wrong bucket).
Still running — but orphaned from Terraform's view.
choices: Enable versioning (minimum) + MFA delete on state buckets + cross-region replication, restrict who can delete (separate permissions from read/write), and rehearse the restore — 'versioning is on' isn't a plan until someone has actually restored from it. The 400-resource re-import is the tuition for skipping this.
Don't run cleanup scripts — the script is the problem.
Keep a local copy of state — the laptop is the backup.
Terraform should prevent deletion — it's a product gap.
scenarios.why: That the blast radius was 'only' operational, not data loss — but every future change is now manual or requires re-import, because Terraform is stateless without its state. Versioning turns deletion into a restore; without it, deletion is forever. Choice 2 bans scripts instead of protecting the bucket. Choice 3 makes the laptop the DR plan. Choice 4 waits for the product to fix the process.
scenarios.hint: What does the running infrastructure prove?

scenarios.title: The $30,000 NAT Gateway
scenarios.situation: A dev environment — used 9-to-5 by 4 engineers — runs a full production-shaped network: NAT Gateway per AZ, 24/7. Monthly cost: $30,000 for an environment that generates zero revenue. Nobody questioned it; 'that's the standard architecture.'
scenarios.prompt: What process would have prevented this?
choices: Pre-apply cost estimation on the PR (Infracost-style plan comments) + a policy distinguishing prod from non-prod shapes (single NAT for dev, scheduled shutdown nights/weekends) — 'standard architecture' is a prod answer applied where it doesn't belong; cost review makes the mismatch visible before the spend.
Cheaper engineers — they should have known.
Delete dev environments — develop in prod.
$30k is fine — dev velocity is worth it.
scenarios.why: Laundering a prod design into dev without the prod justification — the shape was never cost-reviewed for its context. Pre-apply estimates force the question 'does dev need 3 NAT Gateways?' while the answer is still cheap. Choice 2 blames people for a missing gate. Choice 3 is reckless. Choice 4 declines to do arithmetic.
scenarios.hint: What is 'standard architecture' doing here?

scenarios.title: The self-approved prod change
scenarios.situation: An engineer merges their own Terraform PR to production at 6pm Friday — no reviewer, no CODEOWNERS, CI applies automatically on merge. The change opens a security group to 0.0.0.0/0. Nobody notices until Monday's scan.
scenarios.prompt: What layered controls were missing?
choices: Independent required review (CODEOWNERS per directory), no self-approval, approval gate before prod apply (not auto-apply on merge for prod), and policy-as-code blocking 0.0.0.0/0 — any ONE of these likely stops it; the incident needed all four missing simultaneously.
Better engineers — this one was careless.
No Friday deploys — the day is the problem.
Remove auto-apply everywhere — manual applies for everything.
scenarios.why: Defense in depth — each control (review, CODEOWNERS, approval gate, policy) is an independent chance to stop the change; the incident required all four to be absent. Blaming the engineer fixes one person; adding the controls fixes the system. Choice 2 is the blame version. Choice 3 bans Fridays instead of adding gates. Choice 4 throws out dev auto-apply, which was working fine.
scenarios.hint: Why did four missing controls matter more than one careless engineer?

domains.name: Migration Strategies
domains.description: Importing existing infrastructure, state surgery, refactoring into modules, version upgrades, and systematic drift remediation.

scenarios.title: The ClickOps estate
scenarios.situation: A company has 400 resources built by hand in the console over 3 years. Leadership wants it all in Terraform. An engineer proposes: 'Delete it all and rebuild with Terraform over a weekend.'
scenarios.prompt: What is the right approach?
evidence: 400 hand-built resources, 3 years, production, no IaC.
choices: Phased import: inventory everything, prioritize (network/data first — hardest to recreate), import in batches with write-config → import → clean-plan verification per batch, keep the business running — then refactor the onboarded mess. Delete-and-rebuild risks the business for elegance.
Delete and rebuild — it's cleaner.
Leave it — ClickOps works fine.
Import all 400 at once — big bang.
scenarios.why: The business — 400 resources include the ones nobody remembers (that cron job, that bucket policy); rebuild-from-memory guarantees omissions, and the weekend becomes an outage. Import preserves reality; refactor improves it — in that order. Choice 3 surrenders IaC's benefits. Choice 4 batches 400 chances to fail at once.
scenarios.hint: What does 'delete and rebuild' risk?

scenarios.title: The refactor that deleted prod
scenarios.situation: An engineer extracts resources into a module: moves the config, forgets the `state mv`. The next plan shows '3 to destroy, 3 to add.' They apply — 'the plan looked like the refactor.' The production database is destroyed and recreated. Empty.
scenarios.prompt: What is the rule this violates?
evidence: Config moved into module; state addresses not moved.
'3 to destroy, 3 to add' — applied as 'the refactor.'
Database destroyed and recreated. Data gone.
choices: Refactors must produce clean plans — moving config without moving state addresses makes Terraform see deletion+creation; the plan showing destroy/add on a 'refactor' is the alarm, and applying through it is the incident. The discipline: config move + state mv (or `moved` blocks) + verified clean plan, every time.
Modules are dangerous — don't refactor.
The database shouldn't have been in Terraform — keep data out.
Plans lie — don't trust them.
scenarios.why: Terraform couldn't find the resources at their new addresses, so it planned to delete the 'old' ones and create 'new' ones — including the database. A refactor plan must be empty; any destroy/add is the process screaming. Choice 2 bans the practice. Choice 3 exempts the most important resources from IaC. Choice 4 inverts the lesson — the plan told the truth; the human didn't listen.
scenarios.hint: What did '3 to destroy, 3 to add' actually mean?

scenarios.title: The mixed-version team
scenarios.situation: Half the team upgrades to Terraform 1.9; half stays on 1.5. CI uses 1.9. Engineers on 1.5 get state errors; one 'fixes' it by deleting their local state cache, then applies — against a state format their CLI partially understands.
scenarios.prompt: What is the systemic fix?
evidence: Half on 1.9, half on 1.5. CI on 1.9.
State errors on 1.5; a 'fix' involving deleted caches and a risky apply.
choices: Version unity: pin the CLI version everywhere (dev containers / version managers / CI image — one version), upgrade as a team with the staged sequence (dev → stage → prod), and never let mixed versions write state. The 'fix' that deletes caches is how corruption starts.
Let everyone use whatever version — flexibility.
The engineer — don't delete caches.
Stay on 1.5 forever — upgrades cause this.
scenarios.why: State format evolution — newer CLIs may write formats older ones misread, and partial understanding plus a forced apply is corruption with extra steps. Version unity isn't bureaucracy; it's a data-integrity requirement. Choice 2 institutionalizes the hazard. Choice 3 blames the engineer for a missing standard. Choice 4 freezes the toolchain forever.
scenarios.hint: Why is mixed-version state access dangerous?

scenarios.title: The drift that became the standard
scenarios.situation: For a year, engineers 'fix' production by clicking in the console, then update the Terraform config to match — unreviewed. The config now documents a year's worth of unreviewed changes. Nobody knows which were intentional.
scenarios.prompt: What broke, and what is the fix?
evidence: Console fix → config updated to match, unreviewed, for a year.
Now documents 12 months of unreviewed production changes.
Nobody knows which changes were intentional.
choices: The change process — 'codify to match' without review turned IaC into a transcription of ClickOps; the fix is triage discipline (benign drift → PR with review; accidental → revert; suspicious → incident) plus making the fast path the right path (easy PRs, fast applies) so console-fixing loses its appeal.
Terraform — it should prevent console changes.
The engineers — ban console access entirely.
The config — delete it and re-import cleanly.
scenarios.why: A year's worth of unexamined decisions — the review that makes IaC valuable never happened, so the repo is ClickOps with extra steps. Codifying drift is fine; codifying it unreviewed is laundering. Choice 2 asks the tool to fix the process. Choice 3 bans the escape hatch emergencies need. Choice 4 re-imports the same unreviewed reality.
scenarios.hint: What does the config actually document now?

scenarios.title: The upgrade that ate Friday
scenarios.situation: An engineer upgrades the Terraform CLI to a new major on Friday afternoon and immediately applies to prod — 'it's just a CLI.' The new version changed a default behavior; the plan (unread — 'same as always') replaced the load balancer. Outage until rollback.
scenarios.prompt: What are the compounding failures?
evidence: New major CLI, Friday afternoon, straight to prod.
New default behavior replaced the LB. Outage.
choices: Three: upgrading straight to prod (no dev/stage validation), Friday afternoon (no support window), and an unread plan on a version change (when plans matter most). The upgrade sequence exists precisely for this: changelog → dev → stage → prod, with the old version recoverable — and plans get MORE scrutiny on upgrades, not less.
The Terraform team — defaults shouldn't change in majors.
Friday — the day is cursed.
The load balancer — it shouldn't be replaceable.
scenarios.why: Because the tool's behavior changed — 'same as always' is exactly wrong when the version is new; defaults, deprecations, and provider behaviors shift, and the plan is where those shifts surface. Choice 2 blames the releaser for documented changes. Choice 3 bans Fridays. Choice 4 asks the tool to prevent legitimate operations.
scenarios.hint: Why do plans need more scrutiny on upgrades, not less?

lessons.title: IaC Concepts — Core concepts
concepts: Declarative IaC describes desired end state; the tool plans the actions and, crucially, compares current vs desired state on every run — creating only what's missing. Terraform excels at provisioning: declarative lifecycle of infrastructure resources with state.
Drift: mutable patching risks snowflake drift (failed patches, half-applied updates) and rollback means un-patching. Drift is any real-world change made outside Terraform.
Immutable infra means changes produce new images/instances rather than SSH-and-patch, which requires full codification (golden images or IaC) so any instance can be rebuilt identically.
Pets are unique, hand-maintained, and irreplaceable; cattle are identical and disposable.

lessons.title: HCL & Resources — Core concepts
concepts: HCL block types have fixed roles: terraform (version/backend), provider, resource (managed objects, the only ones in state as managed), data (read-only lookups evaluated at plan), variable (inputs), output (exposed values), locals (computed helpers), module (composition).

Count addresses instances by position (aws_subnet.x[0..2]); removing a middle element shifts indices, so Terraform sees changed identities and recreates. for_each addresses by key (aws_subnet.x["b"]), making each instance's identity stable.
for_each: rule: for_each for maps/sets of named things, count for N identical copies.
Variables: together: variables in, locals compute, resources consume, outputs publish.
Validation: variable blocks support type constraints (string, number, list(string), object({...})) and validation { condition, error_message } blocks evaluated at plan.

lessons.title: State Management — Core concepts
concepts: State: backends store state remotely (S3, GCS, AzureRM, Terraform Cloud) with locking (DynamoDB table, native mechanisms) that serializes applies — the second apply waits or fails cleanly instead of corrupting.
Backends: when envs diverge (different resources, backends, access controls), separate directories/configurations (or separate backend keys) give cleaner isolation and blast-radius control.

State locking: import binds an existing real-world object to a resource address in state — it doesn't generate config. 'state mv' (or the declarative moved { from, to } block, which is code-reviewable and applies on next plan) updates the address in place.
Import: for bulk adoption, config-driven import blocks (import { to, id }) in Terraform 1.5+ make it reviewable in code.

lessons.title: Modules — Core concepts
concepts: Module blocks: source (registry address namespace/name/provider, git URL, or local path) + version constraint (registry modules only) + input variables. Module blocks support for_each (and count): for_each over a map gives stable keyed instances (module.app["prod"]), so adding/removing envs only affects that instance.

Module design: version the module so interface changes are explicit. Note: modules with for_each can't be targeted as granularly in older versions, and their outputs become maps — design consumers accordingly.
Interface: keep the interface small and stable; internals (main.tf) can churn.

Module instances: each module block's source+version stands alone; there's no inheritance of version constraints down the tree. A module is an API: variables.tf declares the contract (type, description, default, validation), outputs.tf publishes results (with descriptions, sensitive flags).

lessons.title: Workflows & Cloud — Core concepts
concepts: Workflow: use -target only for exceptional recovery, never as routine workflow.

Plan files: init prepares the working directory (provider binaries, module sources, backend init — rerun after config changes); plan shows the create/update/delete diff for review (the safety gate); apply executes (prompts for confirmation unless -auto-approve). validate/fmt are hygiene steps inside the loop: fmt -check in CI, validate for syntax.

-replace=<addr> marks one resource for destroy+create (taint's successor — 'terraform taint' is deprecated in favor of -replace). -target limits the apply to specific resources — powerful but dangerous: it skips everything else, leaving the rest unmanaged for that run and risking partial-state surprises.

lessons.title: Welcome: How to Use This Bootcamp
concepts: This bootcamp teaches Terraform the way production teaches it: concepts in lessons, judgment in scenarios, muscle memory in labs. Every domain follows the loop: learn it, apply it, run it.

Scenarios mirror real infrastructure decisions: a situation, evidence (configs, plans, state), four choices, one best answer. They test the judgment that separates 'ran the tutorial' from 'can run production.'
Labs are terminal drills: real Terraform CLI commands with checks that verify your output. The lab passes when the checks pass — like a pipeline, the machine is the judge.
Terraform is declarative and stateful — the two ideas everything else hangs on. If you deeply understand 'describe the end state' and 'the state file is the memory,' every other domain gets easier.

Honesty note: Terraform manages infrastructure, but judgment manages Terraform. This bootcamp builds the judgment: when to modularize, how to structure state, what to test, and how to recover when apply goes wrong.

Common trap: skipping explanations on correct answers — a right answer for the wrong reason is a future outage.

lessons.title: How to Navigate: Lessons, Scenarios, Labs
concepts: Lessons teach with worked examples: concepts, an HCL example with a walkthrough, pitfalls, and a try-it. Read actively — predict the plan output before reading the walkthrough.

Scenarios test application under realistic ambiguity: hand-edited resources, drift, state conflicts, module choices. Think like the on-call engineer, eliminate with reasons, then read the full explanation.
Labs rework scenario concepts into CLI commands with verifiable checks. Run every command yourself — `terraform plan` output is a skill you read fluently only by reading it repeatedly.

Domain order is deliberate: concepts → HCL → state → modules → workflows → GitOps, then workspaces, providers, testing, enterprise, migration. Later domains assume earlier ones — state management before workspaces, for example.
The Mock Assessment draws from all domains under timed conditions. Take it after the domains, repair weak areas from the breakdown, and re-take. The second mock is the one that predicts the exam.

lessons.title: How You'll Be Assessed
concepts: Scenario format: situation + evidence (configs, plans, state snippets) + prompt + 4 choices. They test infrastructure judgment — the same judgment interviews probe with 'tell me about a production incident.'
Hints model the question a senior engineer would ask: 'what does the state say?' 'what would plan do here?' Use them while learning; wean off before the mock.
Labs pass on checks: run the commands, match expected output. Like a pipeline gate, there's no partial credit — 'I understand workspaces' without `terraform workspace list` working is not done.
The mock is timed and cumulative. Its per-domain breakdown is your most valuable study artifact — it tells you exactly where to aim repair.
Passing standard: all labs green, scenario accuracy above 75% per domain, mock at target, capstone repo built and defended. That combination predicts real-world readiness.

lessons.title: Capstone Overview: Production-Grade Infrastructure
concepts: The capstone: a production-grade Terraform repository that provisions a realistic stack — network, compute, data, and observability — across two environments (dev/prod) with modules, remote state, CI, and policy.

Required components: (1) reusable modules with clean interfaces, (2) per-environment configuration (no copy-paste), (3) remote state with locking per environment, (4) a CI pipeline that plans on PR and applies on merge, (5) policy checks that block real misconfigurations.
Every decision must reference bootcamp concepts: 'state per environment because...', 'this module's interface is X because...', 'the pipeline plans on PR because...' — the repo is the exam.

Constraints: `terraform plan` must be clean and readable, no secrets in the repo, no hardcoded environment specifics in modules, and a documented disaster story — what happens when state is lost, and how you recover (you will rehearse it).
Deliverables: the repo, green pipeline runs, a README with architecture and decisions, and a 10-minute recorded walkthrough. If a stranger can clone, understand, and safely plan it, it is done.

Pipeline: PR → fmt/validate/plan comment; merge → apply with approval.
Policy: no public S3, required tags, approved regions — blocking.

lessons.title: Presenting and Defending Your Architecture
concepts: The 10-minute walkthrough: repo tour (2 min), a clean plan explained (3 min), three design decisions with reasoning (3 min), disaster rehearsal demo (2 min). Ten minutes forces clarity.
Defend three decisions with bootcamp concepts: why this state layout, why this module interface, why this pipeline shape. 'It was easy' is not a defense; trade-offs are.

Invite hostile questions: 'What happens when two engineers apply at once?' 'How do you add a third environment?' 'Show me the policy blocking a real violation.' A repo that can't answer its failure modes is a demo.
Show the pipeline live: a PR with a plan comment, a policy violation blocked, an apply with approval. Green checks are claims; the blocked violation is evidence.
After defending, write the retrospective: what the bootcamp taught you that the repo used, and what the repo taught you that the bootcamp didn't. That document is the real capstone.

lessons.title: Workspaces: What They Are
concepts: A workspace is a named state partition within one backend: `terraform workspace new prod` gives the same configuration a separate state file. Same code, isolated state — that's the whole idea.

The workspace name is available in configuration as `terraform.workspace`, so you can branch behavior: instance counts, sizes, feature flags per workspace. But branching on it heavily is a smell (see the pitfalls).
Workspaces share everything except state: the same backend, the same credentials, the same provider configuration. That sharing is both the convenience and the danger.
The default workspace always exists and can't be deleted. Convention: never use `default` for real infrastructure — it's where accidents happen when someone forgets to select.
Workspaces are a mechanism, not a strategy. They solve 'separate state, same code' — they don't solve access control, blast radius, or approval workflows. Know what they give you and what they don't.

example.walkthrough: Trace it: `workspace new prod` then `apply` — where does the state file land in the bucket, and what does `terraform.workspace` evaluate to during that apply? What about in `default`?

pitfalls: Common trap: `default` for real infra — the workspace you land in when you forget to select; name your environments explicitly.
Common trap: heavy terraform.workspace branching — `count = workspace == "prod" ? 3 : 1` scattered everywhere becomes unreviewable; prefer tfvars per environment.
Common trap: 'workspaces = environments' — they isolate state, not access, cost, or blast radius; prod deserves stronger separation.
Common trap: forgetting which workspace you're in — `terraform workspace show` belongs in your prompt or your runbook's first step.

lessons.title: Workspaces vs Separate Directories
concepts: Two patterns for environments: workspaces (one config, N state partitions) vs separate directories/configurations per environment (N configs, N states). The choice shapes your blast radius and your workflow.

Workspaces win on: DRY (one codebase), simplicity (no duplication), and small teams. They lose on: blast radius (one backend, one credential set), access control (can't easily restrict prod), and divergent environments.

Separate directories win on: isolation (different backends, different credentials, different permissions per env), divergence (prod can differ structurally), and clear ownership. They lose on: duplication risk — mitigated by shared modules.

The professional default: shared modules + per-environment root configurations + per-environment state. Modules carry the DRY; directories carry the isolation. Workspaces fit small, similar environments.

Migration path: start with workspaces if you must, but design module boundaries so the split into directories later is mechanical. The worst outcome is workspace sprawl with prod one typo away from dev.

example.code:
Worked example — the decision
Startup, 3 engineers, dev/staging/prod nearly identical: workspaces — one backend, simple, fine.
Same company at 50 engineers, SOC 2, prod needs restricted access: separate directories + per-env backends + per-env credentials — workspaces can't express 'only SREs touch prod state.'
Takeaway: the right answer changes with team size and compliance needs — decide explicitly, revisit annually.

pitfalls: Common trap: defaulting without deciding — drifting into workspaces because the tutorial used them; it's an architecture decision.
Common trap: mixed patterns — workspaces AND per-env directories for the same stack; pick one, the confusion isn't worth it.
Common trap: 'we'll split later' without module boundaries — the split becomes a rewrite; keep modules clean from day one.
Common trap: prod/dev in one backend — a dev `apply` bug (or a wrong workspace) reaches prod state; separate backends are the seatbelt.

lessons.title: Per-Environment Variables
concepts: Environments differ in values, not (usually) in structure: instance sizes, counts, domains, feature flags. Those differences belong in variable values — tfvars files — not in branched logic.

The pattern: one root configuration with declared variables, plus `dev.tfvars`, `prod.tfvars` (or per-directory `terraform.tfvars`). `terraform apply -var-file=prod.tfvars` selects the values; the code stays identical.

Never commit secrets in tfvars. Variable values that are secrets go through environment variables (TF_VAR_*), a secrets manager, or a vault provider — committed tfvars are for non-sensitive values only.

Validate early: `validation` blocks on variables catch bad values at plan time ('instance_type must be in the approved list'), long before apply. Per-env tfvars plus validation = misconfiguration caught in CI.

The tfvars contract: every environment's tfvars file sets every required variable (no silent defaults for prod-critical values), and CI verifies it — `terraform plan -var-file=$ENV.tfvars` for every env on every PR.

example.walkthrough: What happens if prod.tfvars sets instance_type = "x9.mega"? At which command does it fail, and why is that the right time?

pitfalls: Common trap: secrets in tfvars — committed secrets are compromised secrets; use TF_VAR_*, vault, or a secrets manager.
Common trap: silent defaults — `default = "t3.micro"` on a prod-critical variable hides a missing tfvars value; require it explicitly.
Common trap: unvalidated variables — a typo in prod.tfvars becomes a 2am apply failure; validation blocks catch it at plan.
Common trap: tfvars drift — dev.tfvars gains a variable prod.tfvars lacks; CI must plan every env, every PR.

lessons.title: Backend per Environment
concepts: Each environment deserves its own backend (or at minimum its own state key with isolated access): separate state files mean a dev accident can't corrupt prod state — blast radius is a design choice.

Backend configuration can't use variables — it's loaded before variables exist. The escape hatch: partial backend configuration with `-backend-config` files per environment (`terraform init -backend-config=prod.hcl`).
Locking per backend: DynamoDB/S3-native locking, Terraform Cloud, or consul — each environment's lock is independent, so a stuck dev apply never blocks prod. Verify locking works before you need it.

State access = infrastructure access: whoever can read/write prod state can reconstruct (and attack) prod. Backend permissions (bucket policies, IAM) are security boundaries — review them like firewall rules.
The init contract: `init -backend-config=<env>.hcl -reconfigure` per environment, documented in the README, enforced in CI. 'Which backend am I talking to?' should never be a mystery.

example.code:
# backend.hcl (per environment — NOT in main config)
# prod.hcl:
bucket         = "my-tf-state-prod"
key            = "prod/terraform.tfstate"
region         = "us-east-1"
dynamodb_table = "tf-locks-prod"
# usage: terraform init -backend-config=prod.hcl -reconfigure
example.walkthrough: Why can't the backend block use variables? What breaks if someone runs plain `terraform init` after a colleague used `-backend-config=prod.hcl`?

pitfalls: Common trap: one backend for all envs — convenient until the dev experiment touches the prod key; separate backends are the seatbelt.
Common trap: variables in backend blocks — Terraform forbids it; the `-backend-config` file is the pattern, not a workaround.
Common trap: untested locking — discovering the lock table is misconfigured during a real concurrent apply; test it deliberately.
Common trap: backend config in git with secrets — backend.hcl files can hold credentials; keep them out of the repo or templated.

lessons.title: Workspace Pitfalls
concepts: Pitfall 1 — the wrong workspace: `apply` in `dev` thinking you're in `prod` (or vice versa). Defenses: workspace name in the shell prompt, `workspace show` in runbooks, CI that derives the workspace from the branch (never from memory).

Pitfall 2 — the leaked resource: a resource created in one workspace referenced by name in another. Workspaces share nothing — cross-workspace references need remote state data sources or explicit outputs, not assumptions.
Pitfall 3 — the destroy in the wrong place: `terraform destroy` is workspace-scoped, which is exactly as dangerous as it sounds. Production destroys require approval gates, not CLI confidence.

Pitfall 4 — the state key collision: two configurations accidentally using the same backend key (copy-pasted backend block). One overwrites the other's state. Key naming conventions + CI checks prevent it.
The meta-defense: make the safe path the easy path. Wrappers/scripts that set workspace + backend + var-file together (per environment) beat documentation that says 'remember to...'

example.code:
Worked example — the Friday incident
Engineer runs `terraform apply` — in workspace `default`, which someone pointed at the prod backend key last month.
Result: dev-intended changes applied to prod.
Post-mortem fixes: `default` workspace banned by policy; wrapper script `tfw prod apply` sets workspace+backend+tfvars atomically; prompt shows workspace.
Takeaway: the incident was a UX failure, not a people failure — fix the UX.
example.walkthrough: Audit your own workflow: how many manual steps stand between you and the wrong environment? Reduce it to one command.

pitfalls: Common trap: 'I'll just remember' — memory is not a control; prompts, wrappers, and CI are.
Common trap: destroy without a gate — `terraform destroy` should be the hardest command to run, not the easiest.
Common trap: copy-paste backend blocks — duplicated keys across configs; template them or check them in CI.
Common trap: blaming the engineer — post-mortems that end at 'human error' fix nothing; fix the system.

lessons.title: Provider Blocks and Versioning
concepts: Providers are plugins that translate Terraform's plans into cloud API calls. Each provider (AWS, Azure, random, time) is versioned independently — and provider upgrades change behavior, so versions are a first-class concern.
Pin providers in `required_providers` with version constraints (`~> 5.0`), not in provider blocks. The constraint is the contract: 'this configuration is known-good with provider X in this range.'

The dependency lock file (`.terraform.lock.hcl`) records the exact provider versions selected. Commit it — it's the guarantee that every engineer and CI run uses identical provider builds. `terraform init` updates it; review the diff.

Provider upgrades are migrations: read the changelog, plan in a non-prod environment first, and expect deprecations to become removals. 'It worked yesterday' after an unpinned upgrade is the most avoidable incident class.
One provider, many versions is impossible in one configuration — but aliases let you configure the SAME provider differently (see next lesson). Version is global; configuration is per-alias.

example.walkthrough: What does `~> 5.0` permit that `= 5.31.0` doesn't, and vice versa? When would you choose each?

pitfalls: Common trap: unpinned providers — no version constraint means every init can pull a new major; the breakage is a matter of time.
Common trap: lock file in .gitignore — then every machine resolves differently; commit it, always.
Common trap: upgrading prod first — provider behavior changes are silent until plan; test upgrades in dev.
Common trap: `>=` without upper bound — permits every future major; constraints should bound the breaking changes.

lessons.title: Aliases: Multi-Region and Multi-Account
concepts: A provider alias is a second configuration of the same provider: `provider "aws" { alias = "west" ... }`. Resources select it with `provider = aws.west`. One configuration, many accounts/regions.

The canonical uses: multi-region (resources in us-east-1 and eu-west-1), multi-account (network account + workload account), and disaster-recovery replicas. Aliases make the topology explicit in code.

Modules and aliases: a module using an aliased provider needs it passed in (`providers = { aws = aws.west }`) — modules don't inherit the caller's aliases implicitly. The `configuration_aliases` declaration makes the requirement explicit.

Alias discipline: name aliases by purpose (`aws.network`, `aws.prod`), not by implementation detail. And keep the count small — each alias is another credential chain to manage and another blast radius to reason about.

The alternative is separate configurations per account/region (with remote-state references between them). Aliases suit tightly-coupled multi-region; separate configs suit loosely-coupled multi-account. Choose by coupling.

example.code:
provider "aws" { region = "us-east-1" }                      # default
provider "aws" { alias = "west"  region = "us-west-2" }  # aliased
resource "aws_s3_bucket" "east" { bucket = "app-east" }                    # default provider
resource "aws_s3_bucket" "west" { provider = aws.west  bucket = "app-west" }  # aliased
example.walkthrough: Which provider configures the `west` bucket's API calls? What credential chain does the aliased provider use — and where would you look to find out?

pitfalls: Common trap: assuming inheritance — child modules don't see the caller's aliases unless passed; the plan error is cryptic.
Common trap: alias sprawl — 12 aliases for 12 regions when 2 would do; each alias multiplies credential management.
Common trap: default-provider ambiguity — resources without `provider =` silently use the default; audit which that is.
Common trap: aliases for environments — dev/prod as aliases in one config shares state-adjacent risk; prefer separate configs.

lessons.title: Provider Authentication
concepts: Providers authenticate to clouds, and the credential chain order matters: static credentials in config (worst) → environment variables → shared config files → instance metadata / workload identity (best). Use the latest method your platform supports.

Never put credentials in provider blocks in committed code. `access_key = "AKIA..."` in git is a breach — rotate immediately, then move to environment variables or, better, workload identity (no long-lived secrets at all).

Assume-role chains: the provider assumes a role in the target account, optionally via another role. `assume_role` blocks with `external_id` (for third-party access) are the standard multi-account pattern — understand whose credentials start the chain.

CI authentication: OIDC federation (GitHub Actions → AWS IAM, etc.) eliminates stored secrets entirely — the pipeline mints short-lived credentials per run. This is the modern default; static CI secrets are legacy.
Debugging auth: `TF_LOG=DEBUG` shows the credential chain resolution; 'no valid credential sources' means the chain is empty, not that your credentials are wrong — check each link in order.

example.walkthrough: Trace the chain: where do the initial credentials come from on your laptop vs in CI? What breaks if the role's trust policy doesn't allow your principal?

pitfalls: Common trap: committed credentials — in git history forever; rotation + history purge, then fix the pattern.
Common trap: overly broad roles — the deploy role with `*` on everything; scope to what Terraform actually manages.
Common trap: 'it works on my machine' — local SSO vs CI OIDC are different chain links; test the CI link, not just yours.
Common trap: ignoring credential expiry — long applies with short-lived tokens fail midway; size token lifetime to the apply.

lessons.title: The Provider Cache and Lock File
concepts: `terraform init` downloads providers into `.terraform/` — the working-dir cache. It's disposable (gitignore it) but its absence means re-download: CI caches it or uses a provider mirror for speed and reliability.

The lock file (`.terraform.lock.hcl`) is the source of truth for WHICH provider builds: exact versions + hashes. `init` selects versions honoring constraints; `-upgrade` re-resolves. Review lock diffs like code diffs.

Provider mirrors: filesystem or network mirrors let air-gapped or fast CI environments install providers without the public registry. `terraform providers mirror` populates one; CLI config points at it.

Version drift between engineers: 'works on my machine' with different lock files. The fix is mechanical — commit the lock file, and CI fails if `init` would change it (dirty lock = unreviewed upgrade).
Plugin cache (`plugin_cache_dir`): shares downloaded providers across working dirs on one machine — big speedup for multi-config developers. Set it once in the CLI config file and forget it.

example.code:
# the lock file workflow
$ terraform init                 # resolves providers, writes .terraform.lock.hcl
$ git diff .terraform.lock.hcl  # REVIEW this: which providers changed, to what?
$ terraform init -upgrade       # deliberate re-resolve (dev first, never prod first)
example.walkthrough: What does each command change on disk? Which files must be committed, and which must be ignored?

pitfalls: Common trap: lock file uncommitted — 'works on my machine' becomes the team motto; commit it.
Common trap: blind `-upgrade` — re-resolving all providers at once; upgrade deliberately, one provider at a time, dev first.
Common trap: committing `.terraform/` — thousands of plugin binaries in git; gitignore the dir, commit the lock.
Common trap: no mirror for CI — every CI run downloads from the public registry; slow and fragile. Mirror it.

lessons.title: Debugging Provider Issues
concepts: The debugging ladder: (1) `terraform version` + `terraform providers` — what versions are actually in play? (2) Read the error fully — provider errors name the API call. (3) `TF_LOG=DEBUG` — the raw API requests/responses. (4) Provider source/changelog — known issues.
`terraform providers` shows the provider requirements tree: which modules need which providers at which versions. Version conflicts surface here before they become cryptic apply errors.
TF_LOG levels: DEBUG shows API traffic; TRACE shows everything including state internals. Logs are huge — reproduce with a minimal config, or grep for the failing resource address.

'Provider produced inconsistent result after apply' means the API returned something different from the plan — usually an API-side default or normalization. The fix is often explicit configuration of the attribute the API defaulted.
When it's really the provider: minimal reproduction + provider version + debug log = the bug report that gets fixed. 'It doesn't work' gets closed; the repro gets patched.

example.code:
# the debugging sequence
$ terraform version && terraform providers   # what is actually installed/required?
$ TF_LOG=DEBUG terraform plan 2>&1 | grep -i 'error\|aws_' | head -30  # the API story
# then: minimal config reproducing it, provider changelog for the version
example.walkthrough: Run `terraform providers` on a real config: which providers appear, and which module introduced each one?

pitfalls: Common trap: skimming the error — provider errors are verbose but specific; the API call name is usually in the first lines.
Common trap: DEBUG on the full config — megabytes of log; minimize first, then log.
Common trap: 'must be my code' — sometimes it IS the provider; check the changelog before rewriting your config.
Common trap: upgrading to fix — sometimes right, but verify the new version's changelog mentions YOUR issue first.

lessons.title: terraform validate and Plan Review
concepts: `terraform validate` checks configuration syntax and internal consistency — no cloud calls, no state. It's the cheapest check: run it first, run it in CI, run it pre-commit. It catches typos, type errors, and missing references.

Validate's limits: it can't catch logic errors, wrong values, or anything requiring provider APIs. 'Validate passed' means 'the HCL is coherent,' not 'the infrastructure is correct' — plan review covers the rest.

Plan review is the human gate: read the plan like a diff. Resources to add/change/destroy, attribute changes, and — critically — anything unexpected. An unexpected destroy in a routine plan is the incident you're preventing.

Saved plans (`plan -out=tfplan` + `apply tfplan`) make review meaningful: the apply executes EXACTLY the reviewed plan, not a fresh re-computation. 'Plan today, apply tomorrow' only works with saved plan files.
The review checklist: (1) resource counts match expectation, (2) no unexpected destroys, (3) changed attributes are the intended ones, (4) outputs look right. Four checks, every plan, no exceptions.

example.code:
# the pre-apply ritual
$ terraform fmt -check && terraform validate   # syntax + coherence
$ terraform plan -out=tfplan                  # review the diff
# ... human reads the plan: counts, destroys, changed attributes ...
$ terraform apply tfplan                       # exactly what was reviewed
example.walkthrough: Why must the apply use the saved tfplan file rather than a fresh `terraform apply`? What could change between them?

pitfalls: Common trap: 'validate passed, ship it' — validate is necessary, not sufficient; the plan is the real review.
Common trap: skimming large plans — 500-resource plans hide destroys; use `plan -target` scoping and tooling, but READ it.
Common trap: plan/apply skew — applying without the saved plan file re-computes; reality may have drifted since review.
Common trap: no checklist — 'looks fine' is not a review; the four checks are.

lessons.title: Static Analysis: fmt, tflint, checkov
concepts: `terraform fmt` is non-negotiable: canonical formatting, enforced in CI (`fmt -check` fails the build). Formatting debates are over — the tool decides, everyone complies.

tflint catches what fmt can't: deprecated syntax, invalid resource types, missing required attributes, provider-specific mistakes. It's the linter that knows Terraform — run it in CI with the ruleset for your providers.

checkov (and tfsec) scan for security misconfigurations: unencrypted storage, public buckets, open security groups, missing logging. They encode the CIS benchmarks — hundreds of checks you don't have to remember.
The pipeline order: fmt → validate → tflint → checkov → plan. Cheap and fast first; each stage gates the next. A fmt failure shouldn't wait for a 5-minute plan to report.
Baselines and exceptions: legacy configs will fail new checks — use skip comments sparingly, with ticket references and expiry. An unjustified skip is a vulnerability with a comment.

example.code:
# the static pipeline (fastest first)
$ terraform fmt -check -recursive   # formatting gate
$ tflint --init && tflint            # Terraform-aware lint
$ checkov -d . --framework terraform # security misconfigurations
# all green? THEN plan.
example.walkthrough: Run all three on a real config: which stage finds what? Categorize each finding as style, correctness, or security.

pitfalls: Common trap: fmt as suggestion — unformatted code in review wastes human attention on what the tool enforces.
Common trap: linter noise — 200 warnings everyone ignores; curate the ruleset until every warning is actionable.
Common trap: checkov as theater — green scan, open bucket (skipped with no ticket); the skip IS the finding.
Common trap: running them manually — if it's not in CI, it doesn't happen; automate the whole chain.

lessons.title: Policy as Code: Sentinel and OPA
concepts: Policy as code turns 'we don't allow public S3 buckets' from a wiki page into an enforced gate: every plan is checked against policy, violations block apply. The policy is versioned, tested, and reviewed like code.

Sentinel (Terraform Cloud/Enterprise) and OPA/Conftest (open source, Rego language) are the two ecosystems. Same idea: write rules over the plan JSON, fail violating plans. Choose by platform, not by hype.
Good policies are specific and actionable: 's3 buckets must have versioning enabled' with the resource address in the failure message — not 'be secure.' The engineer must know exactly what to fix.

Policy tiers: advisory (warn, don't block — for new rules), mandatory (block — for proven rules), and break-glass (override with ticket + expiry + audit). Rolling out a blocking rule without an advisory phase creates revolt.
Test your policies: every rule needs a passing and failing fixture. An untested policy is a gate that might block legitimate work at 2am — or silently pass everything.

example.code:
Worked example — the rollout
New rule: 'RDS instances must have deletion protection.'
Week 1-2: advisory — violations warn, teams fix 40 databases.
Week 3: mandatory — the remaining 3 get fixed or ticketed.
Incident that never happened: the Friday apply that would have replaced a database.
Takeaway: advisory-then-mandatory is how policy gets adopted instead of resented.
example.walkthrough: Write one policy for your stack (e.g., 'no 0.0.0.0/0 ingress'): what exactly does it check, and what's the fix message?

pitfalls: Common trap: policy as surprise — blocking rules with no advisory phase; teams learn about policy from failed applies.
Common trap: vague rules — 'must be secure' is unenforceable; rules name resources, attributes, and values.
Common trap: untested policies — the gate itself needs tests; a buggy policy blocks the business.
Common trap: no break-glass — legitimate emergencies need an audited override; without one, people bypass the system.

lessons.title: Integration Testing for Modules
concepts: Unit-testing Terraform is limited — the real test is `apply` in a sandbox: does the module actually provision working infrastructure? Integration tests apply, verify, and destroy.

The pattern: test fixture (a root config calling your module with test inputs) → apply → assert (check outputs, probe the real resource — does the endpoint respond?) → destroy. Terratest (Go) is the established framework; the terraform test framework (`terraform test` with .tftest.hcl) is the native one.
`terraform test` runs assertions against plans and applies: `assert` blocks on outputs and resource attributes. It's built in, no extra language — start here before reaching for heavier frameworks.
Test the contract, not the cloud: assert your module's outputs and key attributes (the bucket is encrypted, the SG has the right rules), not that AWS works. You're testing YOUR code.

Cost discipline: tests that apply real infrastructure cost money and time — tag test resources, destroy in teardown (even on failure — especially on failure), and run the full suite on schedule, not on every commit.

example.walkthrough: What does `command = plan` test vs `command = apply`? Which of your module's behaviors needs each?

pitfalls: Common trap: no tests for shared modules — the module 10 teams depend on is the one that most needs tests.
Common trap: testing the cloud — asserting AWS behaves; test your module's logic and outputs.
Common trap: orphaned test resources — failed teardown leaves expensive resources; teardown must be failure-proof.
Common trap: plan-only testing — plans don't catch apply-time behavior (API defaults, normalization); test applies too.

lessons.title: The Pre-Apply Checklist
concepts: The checklist is the last line of defense between a reviewed plan and production: a fixed sequence, run every time, that catches what review missed. Checklists beat memory — especially at 2am.

The standard checklist: (1) correct workspace/environment selected, (2) plan is the reviewed saved plan (not a fresh one), (3) backend and state are the intended ones, (4) no uncommitted config changes since the plan, (5) approvals recorded for prod.

CI enforcement: the checklist shouldn't be a wiki page — encode it. Pipeline asserts workspace, uses the saved plan artifact, verifies git SHA matches, and requires the approval gate. Humans follow checklists; pipelines enforce them.

The destroy checklist is stricter: everything above PLUS explicit written approval, verified backups (state + data), and a rehearsed recovery. Destroys are the one operation where paranoia is the correct setting.

Post-apply verification closes the loop: outputs match expectations, smoke tests pass, monitoring shows the new resources healthy. Apply isn't done when Terraform exits 0 — it's done when the system is verified.

example.code:
Worked example — the checklist catch
Apply night: checklist step 4 — 'no uncommitted changes since plan' — FAILS. Someone pushed a tweak after the plan was reviewed.
Action: re-plan, re-review the diff (the tweak changed a security group), then apply.
Takeaway: the checklist caught a plan/review skew that 'looks fine' would have shipped.
example.walkthrough: Write your pre-apply checklist now — then encode one item of it in your pipeline this week.

pitfalls: Common trap: checklist as wiki — unread during the incident; encode it in the pipeline.
Common trap: 'we reviewed it, skip the checklist' — review and pre-apply verify different things (the plan vs the conditions).
Common trap: exit-0 = done — Terraform succeeded but the app is down; verification is part of apply.
Common trap: no destroy checklist — the most dangerous operation with the least process; invert that.

lessons.title: Repo Layouts: Monorepo vs Multirepo
concepts: Monorepo: all Terraform in one repository. Wins: atomic cross-stack changes, one pipeline, shared tooling. Loses: blast radius (one repo's pipeline touches everything), noisy history, access control granularity.

Multirepo: one repo per stack/team/domain. Wins: independent pipelines, clear ownership, smaller blast radius. Loses: cross-repo changes need coordination, duplicated tooling, version skew between repos.

The deciding factors: team topology (one platform team → monorepo-friendly; many autonomous teams → multirepo), blast radius tolerance, and module sharing (both need a module strategy — private registry or git-sourced).
The hybrid most enterprises land on: monorepo per domain/platform team, with shared modules published to a private registry. Team autonomy at the repo level, consistency at the module level.
Whichever you choose: the layout must make the blast radius obvious. If an engineer can't tell what `apply` in this directory affects, the layout has failed — regardless of mono/multi.

example.code:
Worked example — the decision
Fintech, 3 platform engineers, one AWS org: monorepo — atomic changes across network+apps, one pipeline to maintain.
Same company at 200 engineers, 5 product lines, PCI scope: multirepo per product line + private module registry — the payments team's pipeline can't touch retail's state.
Takeaway: the layout follows the org chart and the compliance boundary — decide explicitly.
example.walkthrough: Draw your org's blast-radius map: which teams, which compliance scopes, and where the repo boundaries should fall.

pitfalls: Common trap: defaulting — drifting into a layout; it's an architecture decision with a 2-year half-life.
Common trap: monorepo without CODEOWNERS — everyone can approve everything; ownership is fictional.
Common trap: multirepo without a module registry — copy-pasted modules drift; the registry is the consistency mechanism.
Common trap: layout hiding blast radius — `terraform apply` in a directory whose scope is unclear; make it obvious.
