lessons.title: Remote State and Locking at Scale
concepts: At enterprise scale, state is a fleet: hundreds of state files across teams, environments, and accounts. The problems shift from 'how do I store state' to 'how do I govern, secure, and recover it.'

State partitioning strategy: one state per blast-radius unit (per environment per stack, typically). Fewer, bigger states mean simpler management but bigger blast radius; more, smaller states mean finer control but operational overhead. One state per independently-deployable unit is the sweet spot.

Locking at scale: every state needs a lock that actually works — S3+DynamoDB, Terraform Cloud, or equivalent. Stale locks need a runbook (who can force-unlock, with what approval), because 'just force-unlock it' at 2am is how state gets corrupted.

State access governance: bucket policies + IAM per state prefix, audit logging on every state access, and separation — the team that manages billing state shouldn't read security state. State files contain secrets; treat them accordingly.

Disaster recovery for state: versioned buckets (or equivalent) with cross-region replication, tested restore procedures, and — critically — rehearsed. 'We have versioning on' is not a recovery plan; a successful rehearsal is.

example.code:
Worked example — the stale lock at 2am
CI apply crashes mid-run; the DynamoDB lock stays held. Next apply: 'Error acquiring state lock.'
Without a runbook: engineer force-unlocks, but the crashed apply had partially written — state is now inconsistent.
With a runbook: verify no apply is running, inspect the lock info (who/when), check state integrity, then force-unlock with a second approver.
Takeaway: the lock is a safety device; the runbook is what makes it safe.
example.walkthrough: Write your stale-lock runbook now: verification steps, approvers, and the integrity check before force-unlock.

pitfalls: Common trap: force-unlock as first resort — the lock exists because something might be writing; verify first.
Common trap: one giant state — 'simpler' until one apply touches 2000 resources and the blast radius is everything.
Common trap: unversioned state buckets — no recovery from corruption or deletion; versioning is the minimum.
Common trap: state secrets ignored — state files hold secrets in plaintext; encrypt, restrict, audit.

lessons.title: Tagging and Governance
concepts: Tags are the enterprise's nervous system: cost allocation, ownership, environment, compliance scope — all of it rides on consistent tags. Untagged resources are invisible to finance, security, and automation.
Enforce tags in code, not in wiki: a mandatory tags module or default_tags in the provider block, plus policy-as-code requiring them. 'Please remember to tag' has never worked at scale.
The standard set: Owner (team), Environment, CostCenter/Project, ManagedBy (terraform), and Compliance scope where relevant. Fewer, mandatory tags beat 20 optional ones nobody sets.
default_tags (AWS provider) applies tags to all taggable resources automatically — set it once per configuration. Then policy-check the exceptions, not the rule.

Tagging drift: resources created outside Terraform (ClickOps) arrive untagged. The governance loop is detect (config rules / drift detection) → tag or import → prevent (SCPs denying untagged creation). Close the loop.

example.walkthrough: What happens to a resource type that doesn't support tags? How does your policy handle the exception without becoming a loophole?

pitfalls: Common trap: optional tags — 'recommended' tags are unset tags; make them mandatory via default_tags + policy.
Common trap: 20-tag taxonomies — nobody remembers them; 4-5 mandatory tags, enforced.
Common trap: tagging only in Terraform — ClickOps resources arrive untagged; the detect-tag-prevent loop covers them.
Common trap: tags without consumers — tags nobody queries are decoration; wire them to cost reports and automation first.

lessons.title: Cost Estimation and FinOps
concepts: Every `apply` spends money — cost estimation makes the spending visible before it happens. Infracost (and cloud provider calculators) annotate plans/PRs with dollar deltas: '+$1,240/mo.' Review cost like you review the diff.
The PR cost comment is the behavior changer: engineers optimize what they see. A plan comment showing a $4,000/mo NAT Gateway makes the 'do we need this?' conversation happen BEFORE the apply.

Cost policies as code: block (or warn on) known-expensive patterns — unencrypted... no, expensive: `m5.24xlarge` without approval, NAT Gateway per AZ without justification, unattached EBS volumes. Policy turns FinOps from nagging into gating.

The big levers: right-sizing (most instances are oversized — check utilization), lifecycle (dev environments sleep at night), storage tiers and retention, and data transfer (the silent killer — cross-AZ and egress add up).

FinOps is a loop, not a project: estimate (pre-apply) → observe (cost allocation by tags) → optimize (rightsizing, schedules) → repeat monthly. The tagging lesson is what makes the observe step possible.

example.code:
Worked example — the PR comment
PR: new analytics stack. Infracost comment: '+$3,800/mo — breakdown: Redshift cluster $2,900, NAT Gateway $96, ...'
Reviewer: 'Do we need the Redshift, or does Athena on the S3 data work?'
Revised: Athena version, +$140/mo.
Takeaway: the dollar figure moved the architecture — before a cent was spent.
example.walkthrough: Estimate your current (or planned) stack's monthly cost: which three resources dominate, and what's the cheaper alternative for each?

pitfalls: Common trap: cost as afterthought — the bill arrives monthly; the architecture decisions happened weeks ago.
Common trap: optimizing pennies — hours spent saving $3/mo while the $3,000/mo cluster runs unquestioned; rank by size.
Common trap: no cost accountability — untagged resources can't be allocated; FinOps starts with the tagging lesson.
Common trap: 'we'll optimize later' — later never comes; the PR cost comment makes it now.

lessons.title: Team Workflows and Ownership
concepts: Terraform at team scale is a collaboration problem: who can change what, how changes get reviewed, and how applies happen. The workflow is the product — the HCL is just the payload.
CODEOWNERS per directory: the network team owns network/, the data team owns data/. Reviews route automatically; nobody approves what they don't own. Ownership without CODEOWNERS is aspirational.

The apply authority question: who runs apply on prod? Options: CI-only (recommended — every apply is a reviewed merge), designated releasers, or (never) anyone with CLI access. Decide explicitly; 'whoever feels like it' is how incidents happen.

Branching strategy for infra: trunk-based with short-lived branches beats long-lived environment branches (which drift). Feature branches → PR with plan → merge → auto-apply (dev) / approved-apply (prod).

The on-call contract for Terraform: who responds when the pipeline breaks, where the runbooks live, and what 'revert' means for infrastructure (it's `git revert` + apply — practice it, because infra reverts have state implications code reverts don't).

example.code:
Worked example — the ownership incident
Outage: someone edited network/ without the network team's review — no CODEOWNERS, self-approved.
Fix: CODEOWNERS mapping every directory to a team, required reviews enforced, CI-only prod applies.
Next quarter: zero unreviewed network changes.
Takeaway: the incident was an ownership vacuum; CODEOWNERS + required reviews filled it.
example.walkthrough: Map your (real or hypothetical) repo: directories, owning teams, and who can apply to prod. Where are the vacuums?

pitfalls: Common trap: self-approved infra PRs — the author merging their own production change; require independent review.
Common trap: CLI applies to prod — unaudited, unreviewed, unrepeatable; CI-only for prod, no exceptions.
Common trap: ownership by folklore — 'ask Priya, she knows the network stuff'; write it in CODEOWNERS.
Common trap: no revert practice — the first infra revert shouldn't be during the incident; rehearse it.

lessons.title: Importing Existing Infrastructure
concepts: Import brings ClickOps-built infrastructure under Terraform management without recreating it: `terraform import` (or the `import` block) maps a real resource ID to a resource address in state. The infrastructure doesn't change — Terraform's awareness does.

The import workflow: (1) write the resource configuration matching reality (as close as you can), (2) import to bind the ID, (3) `plan` — the plan shows the gap between your config and reality, (4) refine config until the plan is clean. The plan is the verification.

The `import` block (declarative, reviewable) beats the CLI command for teams: it's in version control, it's part of the plan/apply cycle, and `plan -generate-config-out` can even scaffold the configuration for you.

Import at scale: inventory first (what exists?), prioritize (network and data first — the hardest to recreate), and import in dependency order. Importing 400 resources is a project: batch it, verify each batch's plan, and keep the business running throughout.

What import can't do: it can't generate perfect configuration (you write it), it can't import what the provider doesn't support, and it doesn't fix bad architecture — it onboards it. Import first, refactor second.

example.code:
# the declarative import block (reviewable, repeatable)
import {
  to = aws_vpc.main
  id = "vpc-0abc123def4567890"
}
# then: terraform plan -generate-config-out=generated.tf
# review generated.tf, refine, plan until clean, then apply (no-op) to confirm
example.walkthrough: Why must the plan be clean (no-op) before you consider the import done? What does a non-empty plan after import tell you?

pitfalls: Common trap: import without config — importing into an empty config then writing config blind; write-then-import-then-verify.
Common trap: big-bang import — 400 resources at once; batch it, verify each batch.
Common trap: 'imported = managed' — the config still has to match reality; the plan proves it.
Common trap: importing bad architecture — onboarding the mess is step one; the refactor is step two. Don't skip it.

lessons.title: State Surgery: mv and rm
concepts: `terraform state mv` renames a resource's address in state without touching the real infrastructure: the mechanism behind every refactor (renames, moves into modules, reorganization). The infrastructure doesn't blink — only Terraform's bookkeeping changes.

The refactor pattern: (1) `plan` clean first (baseline), (2) move the config (e.g., into a module), (3) `state mv` each affected address to its new address, (4) `plan` — must be clean again. Any diff means the move was wrong.

`terraform state rm` removes the binding WITHOUT destroying: the resource becomes unmanaged (orphaned from Terraform's view, still running). Use it for resources leaving Terraform management — deliberately, rarely, and with a plan for who manages them next.

State surgery safety: back up the state file first (versioned backend = one click), operate on one resource at a time for big moves (or script carefully), and never `mv` while a teammate might `apply`. Surgery needs a quiet room.
The `-dry-run` habit: for complex moves, practice on a copied state or a dev environment first. State surgery is safe when rehearsed and terrifying when improvised.

example.code:
# the refactor dance: config move + state mv, verified by clean plans
$ terraform plan -out=before.plan     # baseline: clean
# ... move resource into module in the config ...
$ terraform state mv 'aws_s3_bucket.data' 'module.storage.aws_s3_bucket.data'
$ terraform plan                        # must be clean: no adds, no destroys
example.walkthrough: What does a plan showing '1 to destroy, 1 to add' after your mv tell you? What's the recovery?

pitfalls: Common trap: mv without backup — one typo in the address and the binding is wrong; versioned state is the undo.
Common trap: config and state out of sync — moving the config but forgetting the mv (or vice versa); the plan catches it, so READ the plan.
Common trap: surgery during applies — a teammate's concurrent apply mid-surgery; coordinate the quiet room.
Common trap: `state rm` as cleanup — removing the binding doesn't remove the resource; orphaned infra still bills.

lessons.title: Refactoring into Modules
concepts: Refactoring into modules is how configurations grow up: extract repeated or coherent resource groups into modules with clean interfaces. The trigger is usually the third copy-paste — or the first time a change needs making in five places.

The extraction pattern: (1) create the module with variables for everything that differed between copies, (2) replace ONE call site, (3) `state mv` the resources into the module addresses, (4) verify clean plan, (5) repeat for remaining sites. One site at a time — never all at once.

Interface design during extraction: the module's variables are its API. Resist leaking internals (every attribute as a variable); expose intent (environment, size, features). A module with 40 variables is a copy-paste with extra steps.

The `moved` block alternative: declarative refactoring — `moved { from = aws_x.a to = module.m.aws_x.a }` in configuration, handled automatically during apply. Reviewable, version-controlled, and no CLI surgery. Prefer it for team workflows.

Refactoring is a behavior-preserving change: the plan must be empty (or contain only intended diffs) at every step. A refactor that changes infrastructure isn't a refactor — it's a migration wearing a disguise.

example.code:
# the declarative move: no CLI surgery, reviewed like code
moved {
  from = aws_s3_bucket.logs
  to   = module.logging.aws_s3_bucket.logs
}
# after one successful apply with the moved block, it can be removed:
# the state already reflects the new address
example.walkthrough: When would you use `moved` blocks vs `terraform state mv`? What does the moved block give a team that the CLI command doesn't?

pitfalls: Common trap: big-bang module extraction — all sites at once; one site at a time, verified each step.
Common trap: 40-variable modules — exposing every attribute; design the interface around intent.
Common trap: refactor + behavior change together — mixed diffs hide mistakes; refactor clean, then change.
Common trap: no state moves — extracting the module but forgetting the addresses; plan shows destroy/add = data loss.

lessons.title: Upgrading Terraform Versions
concepts: Terraform upgrades are migrations: read the upgrade guide for YOUR version jump (each major has one), test in dev, and expect provider upgrades alongside. 'Just bump the version' is how Friday nights get ruined.

The safe sequence: (1) pin current versions everywhere, (2) read the changelog + upgrade guide, (3) upgrade dev (CLI + providers), (4) full plan/apply cycle in dev, (5) stage, then prod — with the old version recoverable at each step.

State format upgrades: newer CLIs can read old state, but WRITING with a new CLI may upgrade the state format — one-way. That's why the whole team + CI must move together; mixed versions corrupt the workflow, not just the state.

Language changes bite hardest: 0.11→0.12 (HCL2 rewrite), and various deprecations-per-major. `terraform 0.13upgrade`-style tooling automates the mechanical parts; the semantic parts (removed features) need human judgment.

The rollback plan: versioned state + pinned old CLI binary + documented downgrade steps. If the upgrade breaks prod at 2am, 'reinstall the old version and restore state' must be a runbook, not an improvisation.

example.code:
Worked example — the 1.x upgrade
Current: 1.3 everywhere, pinned, lock files committed.
Guide for 1.3→1.9: read (two behavior changes affect us: plan renderer, one deprecation).
Dev: upgrade CLI, `init -upgrade`, full plan/apply — clean except the deprecated argument (fixed).
Stage, then prod, one environment per day. Old CLI binaries kept for a month.
Takeaway: boring, staged, reversible — upgrades should be uneventful.
example.walkthrough: Check your current version pinning: is the CLI version pinned in CI, and is the state format documented?

pitfalls: Common trap: mixed versions — half the team on new, half on old; state writes collide. Move together.
Common trap: upgrading prod first — the behavior change surfaces where it hurts most; dev first, always.
Common trap: skipping the guide — 'it's a minor version'; the guide exists because minors bite.
Common trap: no rollback — the upgrade works until it doesn't; the old binary + state backup is the parachute.

lessons.title: Drift Triage and Remediation
concepts: Drift is inevitable: humans click, automation acts, emergencies happen. The question isn't 'how do we prevent all drift' but 'how do we detect, triage, and remediate it systematically.'

Detection: scheduled `plan -refresh-only` (or drift-detection tooling) on every stack, diffed against baseline, alerted to the owning team. Drift you don't detect is just 'the way things are' until the incident.

Triage categories: (1) benign/intended — codify it (update config via PR), (2) accidental — revert it (apply the config), (3) malicious/suspicious — incident response, not Terraform. Every drift item gets a category and an owner.

Remediation discipline: never hand-edit to match drift and never blindly apply to crush it. Benign drift goes through the normal PR process (reviewed, like any change); accidental drift gets reverted by apply — deliberately, with the team aware.

The drift metric: track open drift items per stack over time. Trending down means the process works; trending up means the guardrails (approvals, education, automation) need work. What gets measured gets managed.

example.code:
Worked example — the weekly triage
Monday drift report: 14 items across 6 stacks.
Triage: 9 benign (auto-scaling tag changes → codify), 3 accidental (manual SG edits → revert via apply), 2 suspicious (unknown IAM changes → security incident).
By Friday: 12 closed with PRs/applies, 2 with security.
Takeaway: triage turned 'drift' from a vague worry into 14 owned work items.
example.walkthrough: Run a drift detection on one of your stacks this week: categorize every item into the three buckets.

pitfalls: Common trap: drift blindness — no detection, so drift accumulates until the plan is unreadable.
Common trap: crush-all-drift applies — reverting benign drift destroys intended changes; triage first.
Common trap: codify-without-review — 'just update the config to match' bakes unreviewed changes into IaC.
Common trap: no metric — drift handled ad hoc forever; the trend line is what drives process investment.

lessons.title: Desired State in Depth
concepts: Desired state is a complete description of what should exist — not steps to build it. Terraform's job is reconciling reality with the description: plan computes the diff, apply executes it. Your job is describing accurately.

Completeness matters: undescribed attributes get provider defaults, and defaults change. The more explicit the configuration, the fewer surprises — 'explicit is better than implicit' is infrastructure law.
Desired state is idempotent by construction: applying twice converges to the same state. This is what makes 'apply' safe to repeat — and what makes hand-edits (unrecorded desired state) so corrosive.

The description must be the whole truth: partial descriptions (managing the VM but not its security group) create shared-ownership hazards. Either manage it in Terraform or explicitly exclude it — the middle ground is where incidents live.

Desired state extends to deletion: removing a resource from configuration means 'this should not exist' — plan shows the destroy, and that's the system working. Deletion as a first-class operation is a feature, not a danger (with review).

example.walkthrough: Which attributes here would get provider defaults if omitted? For each, what could a default change break?

pitfalls: Common trap: minimal configs — three attributes and hope; hope is not a configuration strategy.
Common trap: 'the default is fine' — until the provider changes it; explicit attributes survive upgrades.
Common trap: partial management — Terraform owns the VM, ClickOps owns its SG; the next apply is a surprise.
Common trap: fearing the destroy — removing config shows a destroy in plan; that's the system working as designed.

lessons.title: Idempotence as a Contract
concepts: Idempotence: applying the same configuration N times has the same effect as applying it once. It's the property that makes automation safe — rerun the pipeline, re-run the apply, same result.
Terraform's idempotence comes from state comparison: plan diffs desired vs actual and only acts on the difference. No diff, no action — the second apply is a no-op by construction, not by luck.

Your configurations must preserve it: provisioners and null_resources with timestamps break idempotence (they run every time); data sources that change per-read break it subtly. Every non-idempotent element is a future 'why did apply do that?'

Test idempotence explicitly: apply twice, and the second plan must be empty. Make it a CI check — 'second plan clean' catches provisioner abuse, random values, and timestamp tricks before they reach production.
Idempotence is also the recovery story: after a failed apply, you don't 'undo' — you fix forward and re-apply. The system converges; there's no separate rollback procedure for most failures.

example.code:
# the idempotence check: apply twice, second plan must be empty
$ terraform apply -auto-approve
$ terraform plan -detailed-exitcode; echo "exit: $?"
# exit 0 = empty plan = idempotent. exit 2 = diff present = investigate.
# CI gate: fail the build on exit 2 after a fresh apply.
example.walkthrough: What in your current configs would break the second-plan-clean rule? (Look for timestamp(), provisioners, unpinned data sources.)

pitfalls: Common trap: timestamp() in config — every plan differs; the second apply is never clean.
Common trap: provisioner reliance — scripts that run every apply; move setup into images/user-data.
Common trap: 'apply failed, now what?' panic — fix forward and re-apply; convergence is the design.
Common trap: untested idempotence — assuming it; the double-apply check proves it.

lessons.title: Change Management with IaC
concepts: IaC turns infrastructure changes into code changes — which means they get code's change management: version control, review, CI, and audit trails. A `git log` that shows who changed the firewall and why is the compliance story.

Every change is a PR: the plan output is the review artifact. Reviewers read what WILL happen, not what DID happen — IaC moves review before the change, which is the entire safety improvement over ClickOps.

The audit trail is automatic: git history (who proposed), plan artifacts (what was approved), apply logs (what executed). Auditors ask 'show me the change to prod on March 3rd' — with IaC, that's three commands.

Emergency changes still go through the process — faster, not absent. The break-glass path is: minimal PR, expedited review, apply, post-incident review of why it was an emergency. Emergencies that bypass process become habits.

Change windows and IaC: the pipeline encodes them (prod applies only in windows, with approvals). Policy-as-code enforces what runbooks used to beg for — the process is in the system, not in people's memories.

example.code:
Worked example — the audit
Auditor: 'Who opened port 443 to the world on March 3rd, and was it approved?'
With IaC: git log shows the PR (author, reviewers, plan artifact with the SG diff, apply log with timestamp).
Without: CloudTrail shows an API call from a console session — maybe. The 'why' is gone forever.
Takeaway: IaC doesn't just manage infrastructure; it manufactures evidence.
example.walkthrough: Answer for your stack: 'who changed X on date Y, and was it approved?' — how many commands does it take?

pitfalls: Common trap: PRs without plans — reviewing HCL diffs without the plan is reviewing intentions, not effects.
Common trap: emergency bypass culture — 'just this once' becomes the process; make the fast path the right path.
Common trap: unaudited applies — CLI applies with no log; every apply should be traceable to a person and a change.
Common trap: change windows as folklore — 'we don't deploy Fridays' unenforced; encode it in the pipeline.

lessons.title: Meta-Arguments: count, for_each, depends_on
concepts: Meta-arguments control resource behavior: `count` (N identical copies), `for_each` (one per map/set element), `depends_on` (explicit ordering), `provider` (which provider config), `lifecycle` (create/destroy rules). They're the control plane of HCL.

`count` vs `for_each`: count indexes by number (0,1,2 — fragile: removing element 0 renumbers everything); for_each indexes by key ('web-a', 'web-b' — stable: removing one doesn't disturb others). Prefer for_each for anything that might change.

`depends_on` is for hidden dependencies — when Terraform can't see the relationship from references (e.g., a provisioner needing a DNS record). If you can reference it (`subnet_id = aws_subnet.main.id`), you don't need depends_on — references are the automatic dependency system.

The count/for_each migration hazard: switching a resource from count to for_each changes every address (`aws_x.y[0]` → `aws_x.y["key"]`), which Terraform reads as destroy+recreate. Use `moved` blocks to remap addresses safely.
Meta-argument discipline: for_each over a well-defined map, depends_on only for the invisible, and never count on resources whose membership changes. The meta-arguments shape the plan's stability.

example.walkthrough: Remove subnet "a" from the map: what does the plan show? Contrast with count-based indexing — what would removing index 0 do?

pitfalls: Common trap: count for membership — removing an element renumbers the rest; for_each keys are stable.
Common trap: depends_on everywhere — masking missing references; references are the real dependency system.
Common trap: count→for_each without moved — addresses change, plan shows destroy/add; remap with moved blocks.
Common trap: for_each over a list — lists become sets with unstable keys; use maps (or toset with care).
lessons.try_it: Work through this in the Terminal tab →

lessons.title: Expressions and Functions
concepts: HCL is an expression language: everything (outside blocks) is an expression — references, function calls, conditionals, for-expressions. Fluency here is fluency in Terraform.

For-expressions transform collections: `[for s in aws_subnet.main : s.id]` builds the ID list; `{for k, v in var.tags : k => upper(v)}` builds maps. Most 'how do I reshape this?' questions are for-expressions.
Conditionals (`cond ? a : b`) branch values — use sparingly. Heavy conditional logic in config is a smell: it usually means the difference belongs in tfvars per environment, not in ternaries.

Functions to know cold: `merge` (maps), `concat`/`flatten` (lists), `lookup`/`try` (safe access), `jsonencode` (policies!), `format`/`formatlist` (naming), `cidrsubnet` (networking). The function list is long; these six cover 80%.

`terraform console` is the REPL for expressions: test `merge(a, b)` or a for-expression interactively before committing it to config. Five seconds in console saves twenty minutes of plan-debug cycles.

example.code:
# for-expressions: the reshaping toolkit
locals {
  subnet_ids   = [for s in aws_subnet.main : s.id]                    # list of ids
  subnet_by_az = { for s in aws_subnet.main : s.availability_zone => s.id }  # map az->id
  web_tags     = merge(var.base_tags, { Role = "web" })              # combined tags
  policy       = jsonencode({ Version = "2012-10-17", Statement = [] })  # IAM policies
}
example.walkthrough: In `terraform console`, evaluate each local above against a real config: which ones need real resources, and which work with mock values?

pitfalls: Common trap: ternary sprawl — nested conditionals encoding environments; move it to tfvars.
Common trap: string-building JSON — heredoc IAM policies with interpolation; jsonencode is safer and checkable.
Common trap: untested expressions — committing a complex for-expression untested; console first.
Common trap: `lookup` with wrong defaults — masking missing keys; prefer direct access where the key must exist.

lessons.title: Lifecycle Rules
concepts: The `lifecycle` block controls resource birth and death: `create_before_destroy` (new before old — zero-downtime replacements), `prevent_destroy` (refuse destroys — the safety catch), `ignore_changes` (don't fight external systems on these attributes).

`create_before_destroy` is the zero-downtime pattern: new instance healthy before old terminates. It needs a compatible resource (name conflicts must be avoided — use `name_prefix` or generated names) and it temporarily doubles cost.

`prevent_destroy` is the seatbelt for the irreplaceable: databases, state buckets, key vaults. Plan fails instead of destroying — which forces the deliberate removal of the rule (a reviewed PR) before any destroy. That's the point.

`ignore_changes` is for shared ownership: attributes managed outside Terraform (autoscaling desired_count, external tags). It stops the perpetual diff — but it also stops Terraform from managing those attributes; use narrowly, document why.
Lifecycle is per-resource intent made explicit: 'this must never be destroyed,' 'this must replace cleanly,' 'Terraform doesn't own this attribute.' Write the intent; the block enforces it.

example.walkthrough: What happens on `terraform destroy` with prevent_destroy set? What's the deliberate override path, and why is it designed that way?

pitfalls: Common trap: prevent_destroy as permanent — it blocks legitimate decommissions too; it's a speed bump, not a wall.
Common trap: create_before_destroy without unique names — name collision fails the create; name_prefix or bust.
Common trap: ignore_changes as blanket — ignoring everything hides real drift; scope it to specific attributes.
Common trap: no lifecycle on the irreplaceable — the database without prevent_destroy is one bad plan away from gone.
lessons.try_it: Work through this in the Terminal tab →

lessons.title: Backends: Remote State Done Right
concepts: The backend is where state lives: local (a file — fine for learning, wrong for teams), S3+GCS+Azure (the workhorses), Terraform Cloud (managed), and others. The backend choice determines locking, access control, and durability.

The production backend checklist: remote (not local), locked (concurrent applies serialize), versioned (recovery from corruption), encrypted (state holds secrets), and access-controlled (per-environment permissions). Every item is load-bearing.

S3 backend anatomy: bucket (versioned, encrypted, replication for DR) + DynamoDB table (locking) OR S3-native locking (newer). The bucket policy is a security boundary — review who can read/write/delete like firewall rules.

Backend config can't use variables — use partial configuration with `-backend-config` files per environment. And `terraform init -reconfigure` when switching; the cached backend otherwise lies about where you're writing.

Migrating backends: `init -migrate-state` moves state between backends with confirmation. Back up first, migrate in a quiet window, verify with plan. Backend migration is safe when deliberate, terrifying when accidental.

example.walkthrough: Which of the checklist items (remote, locked, versioned, encrypted, access-controlled) does this block configure, and which live outside it (bucket settings, IAM)?

pitfalls: Common trap: local backend on a team — 'it works for me'; the state file is now a single point of failure and conflict.
Common trap: unversioned state bucket — corruption/deletion is forever; versioning is the minimum DR.
Common trap: variables in backend blocks — Terraform forbids it; -backend-config files are the pattern.
Common trap: stale backend cache — switching envs without -reconfigure writes to the wrong backend silently.

lessons.title: State Locking and Concurrency
concepts: State locking serializes writes: while one apply holds the lock, others wait (or fail fast) instead of corrupting state with concurrent writes. It's the difference between a queue and a corruption.

How locks work (S3+DynamoDB): apply acquires the lock (a DynamoDB item with owner info), writes state, releases. If the process dies mid-apply, the lock stays — stale — and needs the runbook, not panic.

The stale-lock runbook: (1) verify no apply is actually running (CI status, process list), (2) inspect the lock (owner, timestamp — is it yours from the crashed run?), (3) check state integrity (plan should be sane), (4) force-unlock with a second pair of eyes. In that order.

`force-unlock` is the dangerous command: it removes the safety device. Legitimate only after verification — and every force-unlock gets logged, reviewed, and followed by an integrity check. 'Just force-unlock it' is how state dies.
CI and locking: pipelines must handle lock contention gracefully (retry with backoff, or fail fast with a clear message) — and concurrent pipelines on the same state need queueing, not racing.

example.code:
# the stale lock drill (know this BEFORE 2am)
$ terraform plan    # Error: Error acquiring the state lock
$ terraform force-unlock <LOCK_ID>   # ONLY after: verified no apply running,
                                     # inspected lock info, checked state integrity
example.walkthrough: What information does the lock error give you (owner, timestamp)? How do you verify 'no apply is running' in your setup?

pitfalls: Common trap: force-unlock as first resort — the lock might be protecting a live apply; verify first.
Common trap: no lock at all — local backend or misconfigured table; concurrent applies corrupt silently.
Common trap: lock timeouts too short — long applies lose their lock mid-write; size timeouts to the apply.
Common trap: 'it worked without locking' — it worked until two applies coincided; the corruption is a matter of time.

lessons.title: Drift Detection and Remediation
concepts: Drift = reality ≠ state: someone changed it in the console, an autoscaler did its job, an emergency happened. Detection is `terraform plan -refresh-only` (or `terraform refresh` workflows) — refresh the state from reality, diff, report.

The detection cadence: nightly (or per-commit in CI) drift plans on every stack, with alerts to owning teams. Drift detection is monitoring — it needs an owner, a dashboard, and an SLA, not a cron job nobody watches.

Triage before action: benign (autoscaler tags → codify), accidental (console edit → revert via apply), suspicious (unknown IAM change → incident). The categories determine the response; 'just apply' is only right for one of them.

`-refresh-only` plans show drift without proposing changes — safe to run on schedules. The remediation apply is the deliberate, reviewed step that follows triage. Detection and remediation are separate operations with separate approvals.

Drift-proofing: reduce the causes — lifecycle ignore_changes for externally-managed attributes, policy preventing console edits (SCPs), and making the Terraform path the easy path. Detection catches drift; design prevents it.

example.code:
# the drift detection loop
$ terraform plan -refresh-only -out=drift.plan  # what changed out there?
$ terraform show -json drift.plan | jq '.resource_drift'  # the drift, as data
# triage each item: codify (PR) / revert (apply) / incident (security)
example.walkthrough: Run refresh-only on a real stack: how many drift items, and what category is each? (If zero — when was the last real change?)

pitfalls: Common trap: no detection — drift accumulates silently until the plan is fiction.
Common trap: auto-remediate everything — reverting benign drift breaks intended changes; triage first.
Common trap: refresh-only as remediation — it only UPDATES state; the config still needs the codify-or-revert decision.
Common trap: alert fatigue — 200 benign items daily; tune the signal (ignore_changes, filters) until alerts mean action.

lessons.title: Module Composition Patterns
concepts: Modules compose like functions: small, focused modules (network, compute, data) assembled by root configurations. The root is the wiring diagram — it should read like architecture, not logic.

The layered pattern: foundation modules (VPC, IAM) → platform modules (clusters, databases) → workload modules (apps). Lower layers change rarely; upper layers change often. Dependencies flow downward only.
Composition via outputs: module A's outputs feed module B's inputs (`subnet_ids = module.network.private_subnet_ids`). Explicit data flow — no hidden coupling, no cross-module resource references.

The facade pattern: one 'platform' module composing several internal modules, exposing a simplified interface to app teams. Platform team owns the complexity; app teams get `source = "platform"` with five variables.

Anti-patterns: the god module (everything in one — unreusable), the spaghetti (modules referencing each other's internals), and the premature module (abstracted before the second use case — wait for three).

example.walkthrough: Draw your current (or planned) module graph: which modules exist, what flows between them, and are there any upward dependencies?

pitfalls: Common trap: the god module — 'infrastructure' module with 50 resources; decompose by change rate.
Common trap: hidden coupling — modules reaching into each other's internals; outputs are the interface.
Common trap: premature abstraction — module before the second use case; three copies earn a module.
Common trap: circular modules — A needs B's output, B needs A's; restructure (shared module C) instead.
lessons.try_it: Work through this in the Terminal tab →

lessons.title: Versioning and Publishing
concepts: Module versions are API versions: a version bump can break every caller. Semantic versioning applies — breaking interface changes (renamed/removed variables/outputs) require major bumps, and callers pin accordingly.

Version constraints in callers (`version = "~> 2.0"`) bound the blast radius of module updates. Unpinned module sources (`source = "./modules/x"` or bare git URLs) mean every init can pull a breaking change — pin everything shared.

Publishing options: private registry (Terraform Cloud/Enterprise — versioned, searchable, the enterprise standard), git tags (simple, works: `source = "git::https://...?ref=v2.1.0"`), or monorepo paths (fine for one team). Choose by team count and governance needs.

The release process for shared modules: PR → tests (terraform test + integration) → tag/release → changelog → announce breaking changes. Modules are products; their users are your colleagues. Act like it.

Deprecation, not deletion: when an interface must change, ship the new way alongside the old, deprecate with a timeline, then remove in a major version. 'Just update all callers' doesn't scale past three teams.

example.walkthrough: What breaks if the registry publishes v4.0.0 with a renamed output and your constraint is `~> 3.0`? What if it's unpinned?

pitfalls: Common trap: unpinned shared modules — every init is a lottery; pin with constraints.
Common trap: breaking changes in minors — renamed outputs in 2.1.0; semver is a contract, honor it.
Common trap: no changelog — 'just read the diff' across 10 teams; write the changelog.
Common trap: delete-first deprecation — removing before callers migrate; deprecate, timeline, then remove.

lessons.title: Module Interfaces in Depth
concepts: A module's interface is its variables, outputs, and assumptions. Good interfaces are small, intention-revealing, and hard to misuse — the module equivalent of a good API.

Variables: required vs optional (defaults), typed (object types over loose maps), validated (validation blocks catch misuse at plan time). Every variable needs a description — undocumented variables are unusable variables.

Outputs: expose what callers need (IDs, ARNs, endpoints), not everything (no dumping whole resource objects). Outputs are the module's promise — changing them breaks callers, so design them deliberately.

Assumptions are interface too: 'this module expects a VPC with DNS hostnames enabled' must be documented AND validated (preconditions) where possible. Silent assumptions are the bugs that surface at 2am.
The interface review: before publishing, ask 'could a competent stranger use this correctly from the README alone?' If not, the interface — not the stranger — needs work.

example.walkthrough: Audit one of your modules against the checklist: typed variables? descriptions? validations? documented assumptions? outputs minimal?

pitfalls: Common trap: 40-variable modules — every attribute exposed; design around intent, not attributes.
Common trap: undescribed variables — the caller guesses; guesses are wrong at 2am.
Common trap: output-everything — dumping whole objects; outputs are promises, keep them minimal.
Common trap: silent assumptions — 'expects DNS hostnames'; validate with preconditions or document loudly.

lessons.title: The Plan/Apply Pipeline
concepts: The pipeline is the professional workflow: every change flows PR → plan (as a comment) → review → merge → apply (gated). No CLI applies to shared environments — the pipeline is the only writer.
Plan-on-PR is the review revolution: reviewers see the actual infrastructure diff, not just HCL. 'This PR adds 3 instances and destroys 1 database' is reviewable; the HCL diff alone is not.

The apply gate: dev auto-applies on merge (fast feedback), prod requires manual approval (a human confirms the reviewed plan). The gate's strictness scales with the blast radius — that's the whole philosophy.

Pipeline as documentation: the pipeline's stages ARE the runbook. New engineer asks 'how do we deploy?' — the answer is the pipeline definition, not a wiki page. Executable documentation beats written documentation.

Failure handling in pipelines: failed plans block merge, failed applies alert and (where safe) roll back, and every run is logged with the git SHA. 'What did we apply Tuesday?' is answerable — always.

example.code:
Worked example — the pipeline stages
PR opened → CI: fmt/validate/tflint/checkov → terraform plan → plan posted as PR comment.
Reviewer reads the plan: '+3 instances, ~1 SG rule' — approves.
Merge → dev: auto-apply. Merge → prod: approval gate → apply → post-apply smoke tests.
Takeaway: every stage is a gate; the plan comment is the review artifact.
example.walkthrough: Map your current change path: which of these stages exist, and which are 'we'll get to it'?

pitfalls: Common trap: plan without the comment — the plan ran but nobody read it; surface it where review happens.
Common trap: auto-apply to prod — speed over safety for the highest blast radius; gate it.
Common trap: CLI applies alongside the pipeline — two writers, one state; the pipeline must be the only writer.
Common trap: no apply logs — 'who applied what when' unanswerable; log every run with its SHA.

lessons.title: CI/CD for Terraform
concepts: Terraform in CI has specific needs: credentials per environment (OIDC, not static secrets), the right CLI version (pinned, matching the team), a warm plugin cache (or provider mirror), and isolated working directories per stack.

The CI job shape: checkout → setup Terraform (pinned version) → init (backend per env) → fmt/validate/lint → plan (save artifact) → [gate] → apply (saved plan). Each step's output is an artifact; the plan artifact is the reviewable one.

Secrets in CI: OIDC federation mints short-lived cloud credentials per run — no static keys in CI secrets. Terraform Cloud/Enterprise variables or a secrets manager hold the rest. Static CI secrets are the legacy pattern.

Concurrency in CI: two pipelines racing on one state corrupt it — use CI-level concurrency controls (cancel-in-progress for PRs, queue for prod applies) IN ADDITION to state locking. Belt and suspenders.
Drift detection as CI: a scheduled pipeline that plans every stack nightly and alerts on diffs. CI isn't just for changes — it's the watchdog for the changes nobody made.

example.code:
Worked example — the CI anatomy
Job 'plan-dev': OIDC → AWS dev role; setup-terraform 1.9.0; init -backend-config=dev.hcl; fmt/validate/tflint; plan -out=plan.tfplan; upload artifact; comment PR.
Job 'apply-prod': needs: plan-prod; environment: prod (approval gate); download plan.tfplan; apply plan.tfplan.
Takeaway: credentials, versions, and artifacts are all explicit — nothing ambient, nothing assumed.
example.walkthrough: Audit one of your CI pipelines against this anatomy: what's ambient that should be explicit?

pitfalls: Common trap: static cloud keys in CI — rotatable, leakable, legacy; OIDC federation instead.
Common trap: unpinned CLI in CI — 'latest' today differs from 'latest' Tuesday; pin it.
Common trap: racing pipelines — two applies, one state; concurrency controls + state locking.
Common trap: CI only on push — no scheduled drift detection; the watchdog needs a schedule.

lessons.title: Collaboration Workflows
concepts: Terraform is a team sport: the workflows that matter are how changes get proposed, reviewed, applied, and reverted — with multiple humans and one shared state.
The golden path: branch → PR with plan → independent review → merge → pipeline applies. Every step has an owner and an artifact. Deviations (hotfixes) use the expedited path, not the absent path.

Reviewing Terraform PRs: read the plan first (what changes), then the HCL (why this way), then check the blast radius (which environments/stacks). The plan is the primary artifact — HCL review without it is incomplete.

Reverting infrastructure: `git revert` the PR, then apply — but state implications differ from code reverts (destroyed resources don't come back with their data). Rehearse infra reverts; the first one shouldn't be during the incident.

Communication protocols: announce applies in the team channel (who/what/where), especially for shared stacks. 'Applying network changes in 5' prevents the 'who's holding the lock?' mystery — coordination is a feature.

example.code:
Worked example — the revert
Bad PR merged Monday: SG rule too open. Tuesday: `git revert` the merge commit → PR with the revert's plan ('-1 SG rule') → review → merge → apply.
Database note: if the bad PR had REPLACED the DB, revert wouldn't restore data — that's why prevent_destroy + backups exist.
Takeaway: infra reverts work, with state-aware caveats — rehearse them.
example.walkthrough: When did your team last rehearse an infra revert? Schedule one — a bad-PR drill in dev.

pitfalls: Common trap: revert naivety — 'just revert the PR'; destroyed stateful resources need the backup story too.
Common trap: silent applies — nobody knows an apply is running until the lock error; announce applies.
Common trap: review theater — approvals without reading the plan; the plan is the review.
Common trap: hotfix amnesia — the expedited change never gets its post-incident PR; codify it after.

lessons.title: Drift Detection at Scale
concepts: GitOps promises 'git is the source of truth' — drift detection is how you verify the promise: continuously comparing actual infrastructure against the git-defined desired state, across every stack.

The detection architecture: scheduled refresh-only plans per stack (nightly minimum), results aggregated to a dashboard, alerts routed to owning teams. At scale this is a system — with owners and SLIs — not a cron job.

Drift dashboards answer: which stacks drifted, what changed, when, and (via CloudTrail/audit) WHO changed it. 'What changed' without 'who' is half the story — correlate the plan diff with the audit log.

Auto-remediation vs alerting: auto-revert is tempting and dangerous — reverting benign drift breaks intended changes. The mature pattern: alert + triage + deliberate remediation (the migration-strategies triage), with auto-remediation only for narrow, pre-approved cases.

The GitOps drift metric: % of stacks with zero un-triaged drift, tracked weekly. Trending to zero means the process works; plateaued means the triage loop needs investment. GitOps without the metric is aspirational.

example.code:
Worked example — the dashboard that changed behavior
Before: drift found quarterly, in panics, 200 items each time.
After: nightly detection, team-routed alerts, weekly triage metric.
Six months: un-triaged drift items from 200 to 7. The change wasn't tooling — it was ownership + cadence + measurement.
Takeaway: detection is easy; the triage loop is the product.
example.walkthrough: What would your drift dashboard show today? (Be honest — then fix the top 3.)

pitfalls: Common trap: detection without triage — nightly emails nobody reads; route to owners with SLAs.
Common trap: auto-revert everything — reverting intended changes; triage first, always.
Common trap: 'what' without 'who' — the diff without the audit correlation; half the story.
Common trap: no metric — drift handled forever ad hoc; the trend line drives investment.

lessons.title: PR Automation Workflows
concepts: PR automation is GitOps' nervous system: every infrastructure PR triggers fmt/validate/lint, posts the plan as a comment, runs policy checks, and labels risk. The PR becomes a complete decision package.

The plan comment is the centerpiece: human-readable summary (add/change/destroy counts), the full plan collapsed, cost estimate, and policy results. Reviewers decide from the comment — many never open the HCL.

Automation beyond plans: auto-labeling (touches prod? touches network?), reviewer assignment (CODEOWNERS), stale-PR drift warnings ('main moved — re-plan'), and merge-blocking on required checks. The boring work, automated.
The re-plan problem: PRs go stale — main advances, the plan was computed against old main. Automation must detect staleness and re-plan; reviewing a stale plan is reviewing fiction.

ChatOps (optional, powerful): `/plan`, `/apply` from the PR thread, with the same gates as the pipeline. It meets reviewers where they are — but the gates don't move just because the interface is chat.

example.code:
Worked example — the decision package
PR #482: 'Add read replica.'
Bot comment: Plan: +1 RDS instance (db.r5.large), ~0, -0. Cost: +$438/mo. Policy: PASS (deletion protection on, encrypted). Labels: prod, data-team.
Reviewer: reads the comment, checks the cost, approves in 4 minutes.
Takeaway: the automation compressed a 30-minute review into 4 — that's the ROI.
example.walkthrough: What would YOUR ideal PR comment contain? (Plan summary, cost, policy, labels — what's missing?)

pitfalls: Common trap: plan without context — raw plan output, 2000 lines; summarize first, details collapsed.
Common trap: stale plans — reviewing against old main; detect and re-plan automatically.
Common trap: automation without gates — fast PRs that skip policy; speed and safety are both required.
Common trap: ChatOps without audit — `/apply` from chat with no log; every action traceable, always.

lessons.title: Secrets Management in GitOps
concepts: GitOps puts everything in git — except secrets. The rule is absolute: no secrets in the repo, ever. Not encrypted-in-git (usually), not 'temporary,' not 'we'll fix it later.' The repo is the wrong place.

The patterns: (1) secrets manager references (AWS Secrets Manager, Vault) — Terraform reads at apply time via data sources; (2) external-secrets operators — sync secrets into the cluster; (3) encrypted-in-git (SOPS, sealed secrets) — acceptable where the threat model fits, with key management done right.

Terraform specifics: sensitive variables (`sensitive = true`) redact from output, but state files still hold secrets in plaintext — state encryption + access control is mandatory, not optional. `sensitive` hides from humans; the state file needs hiding from everyone unauthorized.

Rotation: secrets referenced dynamically (data sources read at apply) rotate without config changes; secrets baked into state need `taint`/replacement. Design for rotation — 'how do we rotate this?' is a design question, not an ops surprise.
The audit: scan repos for secrets (gitleaks in CI, pre-commit hooks), scan history (the secret from 2021 is still in git log), and have the rotation runbook ready. Assume leakage; verify cleanliness.

example.walkthrough: Trace a secret from creation to Terraform: where does it live at each step, and who can read it? (Include the state file.)

pitfalls: Common trap: 'encrypted in git is fine' — sometimes true, but key management decides; usually prefer the manager.
Common trap: sensitive = secure — it redacts console output; the state file still has it in plaintext.
Common trap: history amnesia — the secret was removed but lives in git log; purge + rotate.
Common trap: no rotation story — 'we'll figure it out'; design the rotation before the first secret.

simulations.brief: A teammate runs terraform plan on the shared staging workspace and the summary reads 'Plan: 0 to add, 0 to change, 1 to destroy.' The database was supposed to be managed. Work the diagnostic steps to find why Terraform wants to destroy it.
simulations.debrief: A destroy plan almost always means config and state disagree about what should exist — removed blocks, wrong workspace, or wrong backend. Diagnose which one before touching anything, and make the correct context explicit in CI.

evidence:

  - aws_db_instance.main  (planned for destroy)

Plan: 0 to add, 0 to change, 1 to destroy.
steps.explain: When a resource block disappears from configuration but the object still exists in state, plan proposes destroy. The fix is to restore the block (or move it intentionally with 'moved' blocks / state mv), not to delete state.
options: The database resource block was removed from the configuration, so Terraform plans to destroy the orphaned real object
The state file is corrupted and must be deleted
The AWS provider version changed and no longer supports RDS
Someone ran terraform taint on the database

choices.feedback: Manual fixes re-create the drift you just codified. Always reconcile through configuration.

Count — Count addresses instances by position (aws_subnet.x[0..2]); removing a middle element shifts indices, so Terraform sees changed identities and recreates. for_each addresses by key (aws_subnet.x["b"]), making each instance's identity stable.
Variables — together: variables in, locals compute, resources consume, outputs publish.

Import — for bulk adoption, config-driven import blocks (import { to, id }) in Terraform 1.5+ make it reviewable in code.

checklist: Get 7–8 hours of sleep the night before — fatigue destroys recall faster than any topic gap.
Bring valid government-issued photo ID and arrive at the test center 30 minutes early.
Eat a real meal beforehand; bring water and a light snack if the center allows them.
Read every question twice before scanning the answer choices.
Flag uncertain questions and move on — return with fresh eyes at the end.
Eliminate the obviously wrong answers first, then compare the survivors.
Budget your time: answer steadily and keep a 10–15 minute review buffer.
Re-run your weakest-domain drill until mastery is at least 80%.
For IaC Concepts: restate the 'why' behind each scenario answer in your own words — if you can't explain it, you don't own it.
Redo one HCL & Resources lab from scratch without looking at the steps.
Recite the key State Management terms from the glossary aloud from memory.
